## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and relevance to heart failure. The strongest signals converge on extracellular remodeling and inflammatory signaling, which are widely regarded as two central processes in cardiac decompensation. Extracellular matrix organization (REAC:R-HSA-1474244, P < 4.76 × 10−22, 62 associated proteins), external encapsulating structure (GO:0030312, P < 4.28 × 10−48, 105 associated proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (GO:0005539, P < 1.28 × 10−15, 35 associated proteins), and endopeptidase activity (GO:0004175, P < 7.23 × 10−14, 57 associated proteins) collectively suggest active matrix turnover, proteolysis, and fibrosis. This pattern is highly consistent with published evidence indicating that maladaptive extracellular matrix deposition, collagen remodeling, and protease-driven structural reorganization contribute to ventricular stiffening, chamber dilation, and progressive loss of cardiac function in heart failure.

Building on this extracellular remodeling signal, the enrichment profile also points toward a substantial inflammatory and immune-associated component. Immune and cytokine pathways were among the most significantly enriched, including cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, P < 3.43 × 10−44, 84 associated proteins), humoral immune response (GO:0006959, P < 7.56 × 10−20, 49 associated proteins), viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, P < 7.04 × 10−21, 35 associated proteins), receptor complex (GO:0043235, P < 6.48 × 10−17, 57 associated proteins), and overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WikiPathways:5095, P < 2.74 × 10−25, 46 associated proteins). Taken together, these findings are compatible with a model in which persistent cytokine activation, immune cell recruitment, and receptor-mediated stress signaling may promote myocardial injury and fibrotic remodeling. Prior studies have consistently linked elevated inflammatory mediators, including interleukin family signaling, tumor necrosis factor signaling, and chemokine networks, with worse cardiac remodeling, reduced contractile performance, and adverse outcomes in heart failure.

In addition to inflammatory signaling, the enrichment results also suggest possible alterations in growth factor regulation and stromal programs. Regulation of insulin-like growth factor transport and uptake by insulin-like growth factor binding proteins (Reactome:R-HSA-381426, P < 2.53 × 10−16, 35 associated proteins) suggests altered growth factor bioavailability in heart failure. This interpretation appears biologically plausible because insulin-like growth factor signaling has established roles in cardiomyocyte survival, hypertrophic adaptation, tissue repair, and fibroblast activation, whereas dysregulation of insulin-like growth factor binding proteins has been associated with cardiac fibrosis and disease progression. Similarly, the enrichment of T cell modulation and desmoplasia in pancreatic cancer (WikiPathways:5078, P < 6.31 × 10−15, 24 associated proteins), although derived from an oncology context, may reflect a shared program of immune activation and stromal expansion that could also be relevant to fibrotic cardiac remodeling.

To further contextualize these pathway-level findings, several phenotype and tissue-enrichment terms provide additional disease-related perspective. Amyloidosis (Human Phenotype Ontology:0011034, P < 8.08 × 10−4, 12 associated proteins) is notable because amyloid deposition is a well-established cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy and heart failure, particularly in infiltrative cardiac disease. Regulation of micro ribonucleic acid transcription (GO:1902893, P < 4.67 × 10−3, 9 associated proteins) may reflect post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms that have been widely implicated in hypertrophy, fibrosis, and inflammation in failing hearts. Overall, the convergence of highly significant pathways spanning extracellular matrix remodeling, cytokine-driven inflammation, receptor signaling, proteolysis, and growth factor regulation is consistent with the current literature view that heart failure involves not only impaired pump function, but also coordinated immune, fibrotic, and tissue-remodeling programs.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Hemoptysis (HP:0002105) 

Hemoptysis refers to the expectoration of blood or blood-streaked sputum originating from the lower respiratory tract, including the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and pulmonary parenchyma. It is a clinical manifestation rather than a discrete molecular signaling pathway, and it reflects disruption of the integrity of the pulmonary vascular or airway mucosal interface. The biological basis of hemoptysis commonly involves elevated pulmonary vascular pressure, inflammation, infection, vascular injury, capillary rupture, bronchial arterial hypertrophy, coagulation abnormalities, or direct destruction of lung tissue. In cardiovascular disease, especially in the setting of left-sided cardiac dysfunction, pulmonary venous congestion can increase hydrostatic pressure within the pulmonary capillary bed, promoting transudation of fluid into the alveolar spaces and, in more severe cases, leakage of red blood cells into the airspaces. This process may produce blood-tinged sputum and, when substantial, clinically apparent hemoptysis. Thus, hemoptysis is best understood as a downstream clinical consequence of cardiopulmonary hemodynamic disturbance, particularly when cardiac dysfunction causes pulmonary congestion, pulmonary edema, and secondary injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier.

Building on this physiological framework, the relationship between hemoptysis and heart failure can be interpreted most plausibly through hemodynamic and barrier-injury mechanisms rather than through a single disease-defining molecular process. No relevant publications were provided for direct citation-based analysis. Nevertheless, in the context of heart failure, hemoptysis is most plausibly related to elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures caused by impaired cardiac pumping or filling. This hemodynamic disturbance leads to pulmonary congestion and increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, which can damage the alveolar-capillary membrane and allow erythrocytes to enter the alveolar spaces, resulting in blood-streaked sputum or overt expectoration of blood. In acute decompensated heart failure, this process may accompany pulmonary edema, where frothy sputum can become pink because of admixture with blood. In more advanced or chronic disease, sustained pulmonary venous hypertension may also contribute to vascular remodeling and fragility, further predisposing to bleeding within the lung. Hemoptysis in heart failure is therefore not usually considered a primary disease-defining feature, but rather a clinically important manifestation of severe pulmonary venous congestion and cardiogenic pulmonary injury. Because hemoptysis also has many non-cardiac causes, including infection, malignancy, pulmonary embolic disease, and inflammatory lung disorders, its presence in a patient with heart failure should prompt careful differential evaluation while recognizing that worsening cardiac dysfunction can be a direct contributing mechanism.

Against this clinical background, the enrichment results provide a quantitative basis for considering how heart failure-associated biology may intersect with mechanisms relevant to hemoptysis. There were 16 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the function related to hemoptysis, a clinical manifestation reflecting disruption of the pulmonary vascular and airway interface under conditions such as pulmonary venous congestion, elevated hydrostatic pressure, alveolar-capillary barrier injury, and red blood cell leakage into the airspaces. This enrichment across 16 proteins supports a quantitatively substantial connection between heart failure biology and cardiopulmonary mechanisms that can contribute to blood-tinged sputum or overt expectoration of blood through pressure-driven and injury-associated processes in the lower respiratory tract. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 16 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

To further clarify the biological relevance of this 16-protein set, the most significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis are introduced below in a more detailed and connected manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, ELN has the most direct and compelling connection to heart failure because it is a fundamental determinant of vascular elasticity and large-vessel integrity. Elastin is essential for the compliance of the aorta and other elastic arteries; disruption of elastic fiber formation or elastin cross-linking can increase arterial stiffness, elevate afterload, and thereby promote adverse cardiac remodeling, a major driver of heart failure progression. The reported roles of ELN in smooth muscle cell maturation, aortic wall integrity, and collagen/elastin cross-linking further indicate that it participates in structural homeostasis of the cardiovascular extracellular matrix. These functions are highly relevant to heart failure pathophysiology, particularly in settings characterized by vascular stiffening, hypertensive remodeling, and impaired ventriculo-arterial coupling. In addition, its regulation of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation through angiotensin signaling links ELN to neurohormonal pathways that are central to heart failure biology. Collectively, ELN stands out as a key matrix regulator whose dysfunction could contribute to both vascular and myocardial mechanical abnormalities associated with heart failure.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

In a closely related structural context, MFAP5 may be considered alongside ELN because both proteins are associated with extracellular matrix architecture and vessel wall mechanics. MFAP5 is noteworthy in the context of heart failure because it is structurally and functionally linked to the elastin-microfibril network, which is essential for vascular resilience and extracellular matrix organization. Although the annotation is less extensive than that for ELN, its localization to elastin-associated microfibrils and its proposed role in maintaining large-vessel integrity suggest that MFAP5 may influence arterial compliance and vessel wall stability. These processes are relevant to heart failure because abnormalities in the vascular extracellular matrix can increase pulsatile load and contribute to chronic pressure stress on the heart. Moreover, the potential involvement of MFAP5 in growth factor regulation and cell signaling raises the possibility that it participates in remodeling pathways that affect both vascular and cardiac tissue homeostasis. Therefore, MFAP5 stands out as a plausible extracellular matrix-associated contributor to the biomechanical and remodeling abnormalities that accompany heart failure.[PubMed:8557636](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8557636) 

Whereas ELN and MFAP5 are most readily interpreted through structural and biomechanical mechanisms, PRTN3 may be more relevant to inflammatory injury and matrix degradation. PRTN3 is particularly relevant to heart failure because it connects inflammation, leukocyte trafficking, endothelial function, and extracellular matrix degradation. Heart failure is increasingly recognized as a syndrome involving chronic sterile inflammation and vascular dysfunction, and PRTN3 has the capacity to amplify these processes. Its proteolytic activity against elastin and several collagenous and adhesive matrix substrates suggests a mechanism by which excessive neutrophil activation could destabilize vascular or interstitial extracellular matrix architecture, thereby contributing to adverse remodeling. In parallel, its roles in neutrophil transendothelial migration and inflammatory signaling indicate that it may facilitate leukocyte infiltration into injured cardiovascular tissues. Although one reported function is enhancement of endothelial barrier integrity via PAR-2 activation during neutrophil migration, this should be interpreted within the broader context of inflammatory vascular responses. Overall, PRTN3 stands out as an inflammation-associated protease with plausible relevance to heart failure progression through matrix injury, endothelial perturbation, and innate immune activation.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Extending this inflammatory perspective, CLEC7A may also be relevant because its annotated functions converge on immune activation and oxidative stress pathways that are often discussed in heart failure biology. CLEC7A is relevant to heart failure primarily through its immunoinflammatory functions. Activation of NF-kappa-B and p38 MAPK signaling, induction of cytokines and chemokines, and promotion of reactive oxygen species generation are all mechanisms strongly implicated in cardiac remodeling and heart failure progression. Inflammatory activation of myeloid cells and oxidative stress can exacerbate myocardial injury, impair contractile function, and stimulate fibrotic remodeling. Although CLEC7A is classically studied in antifungal and innate immune responses, its ability to drive potent inflammatory cascades makes it a biologically plausible contributor to the systemic and tissue-level inflammation observed in heart failure, especially in patients with comorbid infection, immune activation, or heightened innate immune signaling. Thus, CLEC7A stands out as an immune receptor whose downstream pathways intersect with established mechanisms of heart failure pathogenesis.[PubMed:11544516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11544516) [PubMed:15213161](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15213161) [PubMed:17159984](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17159984) [PubMed:12719479](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12719479) [PubMed:15731053](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15731053) [PubMed:16825490](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16825490) [PubMed:32358020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32358020) [PubMed:15845454](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15845454) [PubMed:15729357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15729357) [PubMed:10779524](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10779524) [PubMed:27288407](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27288407) 

In comparison with the preceding proteins, FAS may have a less direct relationship to cardiovascular structure or pulmonary vascular injury, but it may still warrant consideration through cell death and stress-response pathways. FAS may have a more indirect but still potentially meaningful relationship with heart failure through its roles in apoptosis-related signaling and transcriptional control. Cardiomyocyte survival and regulated cell death are central determinants of heart failure development, and the reported ability of this kinase to influence apoptosis via FADD phosphorylation suggests possible relevance to myocardial cell fate decisions under stress. In addition, its effects on JUN-dependent transcription imply a connection to stress-responsive signaling networks that can govern hypertrophy, inflammation, and remodeling. The annotation also highlights steroidogenic and hormone-responsive transcriptional functions, which may be pertinent because endocrine signaling can modulate cardiovascular remodeling and fluid homeostasis. However, compared with ELN, MFAP5, PRTN3, and CLEC7A, the direct evidence linking this protein to cardiovascular structural or inflammatory mechanisms is less specific. Therefore, it is best considered a secondary candidate whose mechanistic relevance to heart failure would likely depend on context-specific regulation of apoptosis and stress signaling.

Finally, CEACAM6 appears to be the least directly connected to the central hemodynamic, extracellular matrix, or inflammatory themes outlined above, and its relevance should therefore be interpreted more cautiously. CEACAM6 appears to have the weakest direct connection to heart failure among the listed proteins. Its annotated functions are centered on epithelial cell adhesion, oncogenic signaling, and tumor progression, particularly resistance to anoikis in colorectal carcinoma cells. While cell adhesion molecules can sometimes influence inflammatory signaling or vascular interactions, the provided functional evidence does not indicate a clear role in cardiovascular structure, hemodynamics, extracellular matrix remodeling, or canonical heart failure pathways. Accordingly, CEACAM6 is less likely to represent a primary heart failure-related candidate based on the current annotations alone. Any relevance would be speculative and probably indirect, for example through broader effects on systemic inflammation or comorbidity burden rather than a direct mechanistic role in heart failure pathogenesis.

### Colon; goblet cells[≥Low] (HPA:0130891) 

This pathway label refers to a cell type feature rather than a canonical intracellular signaling cascade. Goblet cells are specialized secretory epithelial cells of the colon that synthesize and release mucins and other protective factors to maintain the intestinal mucus barrier. Through production of the mucus layer, goblet cells contribute to spatial separation between luminal microorganisms and the intestinal epithelium, limit microbial translocation, and participate in regulation of local immune homeostasis. Accordingly, a designation of low goblet cell abundance in the colon may indicate reduced mucus barrier support, greater vulnerability to epithelial barrier dysfunction, altered host and microbial interactions, and an increased likelihood of intestinal inflammation and systemic exposure to microbial products. In a broader pathophysiological framework, the colon and its epithelial secretory cell populations are increasingly recognized as components of the heart failure associated gut axis, in which intestinal hypoperfusion, venous congestion, barrier injury, microbiota disturbance, and immune activation may contribute to systemic inflammation and progression of cardiac dysfunction.

With this biological context in mind, the relevance of this feature to heart failure can be considered even though direct pathway-specific evidence was not supplied. No pathway specific publications were provided, so a direct literature based attribution for this exact pathway label cannot be made from the supplied evidence. Nevertheless, the biological relevance of low colonic goblet cell representation to heart failure can be inferred from the established concept that heart failure is associated with intestinal congestion, reduced perfusion, epithelial barrier impairment, and increased passage of microbial products into the circulation. Because goblet cells are central to preservation of the colonic mucus barrier, a reduction in these cells would be expected to weaken mucosal defense, facilitate contact between luminal microorganisms and the epithelium, and amplify intestinal and systemic inflammatory signaling. Such processes are highly pertinent to heart failure, in which chronic inflammation, immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, and adverse cardiac remodeling are important determinants of disease severity and progression. Thus, even in the absence of publications directly linked to this pathway entry, low goblet cell abundance in the colon is plausibly related to heart failure as a marker or mediator of gut barrier failure within the intestinal and cardiac axis, potentially contributing to systemic inflammatory burden and worsening cardiovascular outcomes. Because no relevant publications were supplied, this interpretation should be regarded as mechanistic and hypothesis generating rather than citation supported for this specific pathway annotation.

Building on this mechanistic interpretation, the enrichment results provide a quantitative perspective on the possible connection between this colonic epithelial feature and heart failure biology. There were 40 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing low goblet cell abundance in the colon, a feature that reflects reduced epithelial secretory barrier support rather than a canonical intracellular signaling cascade. This enrichment therefore points to a quantitative connection between heart failure and intestinal barrier related biology, with the 40 protein set supporting a disease framework in which impaired mucus layer maintenance, increased epithelial vulnerability, altered host and microbial interaction, and heightened inflammatory exposure may contribute to progression of systemic pathophysiology in heart failure. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 40 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network inspection and functional exploration.
