To further clarify the biological meaning of this enrichment pattern, the most significant proteins are discussed below in relation to mechanisms that may be relevant to heart failure. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

BNIP3L is one of the most compelling heart failure relevant proteins in this list because mitochondrial dysfunction and cardiomyocyte loss are central drivers of cardiac remodeling and pump failure. Its annotated functions connect two major pathogenic axes in heart failure: apoptosis and mitochondrial quality control. Excessive activation of BNIP3L mediated cell death could contribute to cardiomyocyte depletion, whereas its role in mitochondrial surveillance may be protective under conditions of mitochondrial stress. This duality is especially relevant in the failing heart, where chronic ischemia, oxidative stress, and impaired bioenergetics create sustained mitochondrial damage. Thus, BNIP3L stands out as a plausible regulator of the balance between adaptive mitophagy like quality control and maladaptive cardiomyocyte death, both of which are mechanistically linked to progression of heart failure.

Closely related to this mitochondrial theme, CHCHD10 may also be relevant because the myocardium is exceptionally dependent on intact mitochondrial architecture for adenosine triphosphate production. CHCHD10 is highly relevant to heart failure because the myocardium is exceptionally dependent on intact mitochondrial architecture for ATP production. Maintenance of cristae structure is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, and disruption of mitochondrial ultrastructure is a well recognized feature of failing cardiomyocytes. Even though the annotation is concise, the biological implication is substantial: defects in CHCHD10 associated mitochondrial organization could impair respiratory chain efficiency, increase reactive oxygen species generation, and reduce energetic reserve, thereby exacerbating contractile dysfunction. Proteins governing mitochondrial integrity are of particular interest in heart failure pathogenesis because energetic insufficiency is a hallmark of disease progression.

In parallel with mitochondrial dysfunction, vascular dysregulation represents another major component of heart failure pathophysiology, which makes DDAH1 noteworthy in this context. DDAH1 has a meaningful connection to heart failure through its central role in nitric oxide biology. By degrading ADMA and MMA, DDAH1 relieves inhibition of nitric oxide synthase and supports nitric oxide production, which is critical for endothelial function, vascular tone regulation, myocardial perfusion, and ventricular vascular coupling. In heart failure, endothelial dysfunction and impaired nitric oxide signaling contribute to increased afterload, microvascular dysregulation, and adverse remodeling. Therefore, reduced DDAH1 activity could promote accumulation of NOS inhibitors, worsen vascular dysfunction, and aggravate cardiac stress. Among the listed proteins, DDAH1 is especially notable because it links metabolic regulation of nitric oxide directly to hemodynamic and vascular mechanisms relevant to heart failure.

A related aspect of cardiovascular adaptation involves angiogenesis and extracellular matrix signaling, bringing COL18A1 into focus. COL18A1 is relevant to heart failure because myocardial adaptation to injury and pressure overload depends in part on adequate vascular remodeling and angiogenic support. Its anti angiogenic activity, including inhibition of VEGFA mediated endothelial proliferation and migration, suggests that elevated COL18A1 derived signaling could limit compensatory capillary growth in stressed myocardium. Inadequate angiogenesis is increasingly recognized as a contributor to myocardial hypoxia, fibrosis, and transition from compensated hypertrophy to overt heart failure. The integrin related effects of COL18A1 may further influence extracellular matrix signaling and endothelial behavior, processes that are tightly coupled to adverse cardiac remodeling. Thus, this protein stands out as a potential modulator of the myocardial vascular response in heart failure.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

Beyond vascular remodeling, inflammatory and metabolic stress pathways are also strongly represented in the enriched protein set, and LCN2 appears notable within that broader framework. LCN2 is particularly noteworthy in the context of heart failure because it intersects inflammation, iron metabolism, apoptosis, and cardiorenal biology. These processes are all highly relevant to heart failure syndromes, especially in patients with systemic inflammation, renal dysfunction, and disturbed iron handling. Its ability to modulate intracellular iron availability may influence oxidative stress and cell survival, while its pro apoptotic effects under certain conditions suggest a potential role in tissue injury. Moreover, because renal dysfunction is a major determinant of heart failure progression, a protein implicated in both renal biology and inflammatory responses is of substantial translational interest. LCN2 therefore stands out as a plausible biomarker and mediator at the interface of cardiac stress, immune activation, and cardiorenal syndrome.[PubMed:12453413](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12453413) [PubMed:15531878](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15531878) [PubMed:16446425](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16446425) 

Consistent with this inflammatory dimension, LGALS3 may be especially relevant because it connects immune activation with tissue remodeling. LGALS3 is one of the strongest heart failure related candidates in this list because it is functionally linked to inflammation, tissue remodeling, and cellular stress responses, all of which are central to the pathogenesis of chronic heart failure. Its roles in monocyte or macrophage chemoattraction, neutrophil activation, and clearance of apoptotic cells indicate a capacity to shape the inflammatory milieu that drives fibrotic remodeling and ventricular dysfunction. In addition, its effects on endothelial cell migration suggest relevance to vascular remodeling, and its participation in autophagy related membrane damage responses may influence cardiomyocyte stress adaptation. Although the annotation does not explicitly mention the heart, the convergence of inflammatory, reparative, and stress response functions makes LGALS3 especially important in the context of adverse remodeling and progression of heart failure.

From inflammatory remodeling, the discussion naturally extends to proteolytic homeostasis and lysosomal processing, where LGMN may have potential relevance. LGMN may be relevant to heart failure through its integration of lysosomal function, immune processing, and growth factor receptor turnover. Lysosomal dysfunction and impaired proteostasis are increasingly recognized in failing myocardium, where accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles contributes to cardiomyocyte dysfunction. In addition, the ability of LGMN to regulate EGFR degradation suggests a possible influence on proliferative and survival signaling pathways that can affect fibroblasts, endothelial cells, or inflammatory cells within the remodeling heart. Its role in antigen presentation also points to a potential contribution to immune activation, which is increasingly implicated in nonischemic and ischemic heart failure. Thus, LGMN is a mechanistically interesting candidate linking proteolytic homeostasis and inflammation to disease progression.[PubMed:23776206](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23776206) [PubMed:9872320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9872320) 

In addition to inflammatory and proteostatic mechanisms, systemic metabolic remodeling may also contribute to disease progression, which provides a rationale for considering FABP1. FABP1 is potentially relevant to heart failure because altered systemic and myocardial lipid metabolism are common features of cardiometabolic disease and heart failure progression. Although FABP1 is classically associated with hepatocellular lipid handling, its functions in cholesterol and fatty acid trafficking make it interesting in the broader context of metabolic remodeling, which strongly influences cardiac energetics. Perturbations in lipid transport and substrate utilization can contribute to lipotoxicity, inflammation, and impaired energy production, all of which can worsen cardiac function. FABP1 may therefore be most relevant in heart failure associated with metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes, or congestive hepatopathy, where extracardiac metabolic disturbances feed back on the failing heart.

Compared with the proteins discussed above, GSN appears to have a more indirect and exploratory connection to heart failure biology. Although the annotation is limited, GSN may still be of interest in heart failure because stem or progenitor cell behavior and inflammatory cell turnover can influence myocardial repair and remodeling after injury. If GSN restrains progenitor cell proliferation or differentiation, it could theoretically affect regenerative or immune responses relevant to post injury remodeling. However, compared with other proteins in this list, the direct mechanistic link to heart failure is less immediate. It is therefore a secondary candidate rather than a primary one, but it may still warrant consideration in studies focused on reparative biology or bone marrow cardiac crosstalk.[PubMed:7694679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7694679) 

Another signaling oriented candidate in this enriched set is YAP1, which may be relevant to growth control and stress adaptation in the heart. YAP1 is potentially important in heart failure because Hippo YAP signaling and ERBB family signaling are both implicated in cardiomyocyte survival, growth control, and tissue remodeling. Although the provided annotation is brief, activation of ERBB4 related signaling suggests a connection to pathways involved in myocardial stress adaptation and cell fate regulation. In the heart, dysregulation of growth and survival signaling can determine whether remodeling remains compensatory or becomes maladaptive. Accordingly, YAP1 stands out as a plausible signaling regulator with relevance to cardiac remodeling, even though the specific annotation here is narrower than for several other proteins.

Finally, CKAP4 may also have indirect relevance, although the current functional information suggests a lower priority interpretation. CKAP4 may have indirect relevance to heart failure through its involvement in antiproliferative signaling and possible intersection with Wnt or FZD related pathways, which are important in cardiac remodeling and fibrosis. While the annotation is not heart specific, antiproliferative signaling can be relevant to fibroblast activation, endothelial adaptation, and tissue repair responses. However, compared with proteins directly linked to mitochondrial quality control, nitric oxide regulation, inflammation, or angiogenesis, CKAP4 should be considered a lower priority candidate for heart failure relevance based on the current functional information alone.

### Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (HPA:0381223) 

Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] refers to a placental cellular surface specialization characterized by abundant microvilli on the apical membrane of syncytiotrophoblasts. Syncytiotrophoblasts form the multinucleated outer epithelial layer of the chorionic villi and are directly bathed by maternal blood. Their dense microvillous border greatly expands membrane surface area and supports maternal to fetal exchange of oxygen, nutrients, electrolytes, lipids, hormones, and waste products. This compartment is also enriched in transporters, receptors, ion handling proteins, endocytic machinery, metabolic enzymes, and signaling systems that regulate placental barrier function, endocrine activity, and immunologic interactions at the maternal fetal interface. In biologic pathway annotation, a designation such as this usually indicates genes or proteins with relatively high expression in the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous domain, rather than a single canonical signaling cascade. Therefore, the pathway is best understood as a tissue and subcellular localization signature linked to placental transport, membrane remodeling, vesicular trafficking, and maternal fetal homeostasis.

With this biologic context in mind, the relevance of this signature to heart failure should be interpreted cautiously and in a largely indirect framework. No relevant publications were provided, and the named pathway is a placenta specific localization signature rather than an established heart failure pathway. Accordingly, there is no direct literature based evidence available here to support a specific mechanistic link between high expression in syncytiotrophoblast microvilli and heart failure. From a biologic perspective, any relationship to heart failure would most plausibly be indirect and context dependent. Placental microvillous function is central to maternal fetal exchange and to the production of endocrine and vasoactive factors that influence maternal hemodynamics, vascular tone, inflammation, and metabolic adaptation during pregnancy. Disturbance of these placental processes can contribute to pregnancy complications associated with increased cardiovascular stress, and such conditions may precipitate or unmask heart failure in susceptible individuals during pregnancy or the postpartum period. However, without pathway specific publications, one cannot conclude that this placental signature has an intrinsic or direct role in the pathogenesis of heart failure outside pregnancy related contexts. Thus, the most rigorous interpretation is that this pathway currently has no demonstrated direct association with heart failure based on the evidence supplied, and any proposed connection remains inferential and should be validated with targeted studies and relevant citations.

Even so, the enrichment results suggest that this localization signature may still capture molecular features that overlap with processes relevant to heart failure biology. There were 27 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High], indicating that this localization signature captures a measurable subset of the disease-related protein set and supports a biologically relevant connection between heart failure and molecular programs linked to membrane surface specialization, transmembrane transport, vesicular trafficking, barrier regulation, and maternal fetal exchange functions. Given that the annotated compartment is defined by abundant apical microvilli on syncytiotrophoblasts, the enrichment of 27 proteins suggests overrepresentation of proteins associated with high-capacity membrane dynamics, ion and solute handling, receptor-mediated signaling, endocytic activity, and metabolic processing, all of which are processes that can also be mechanistically relevant to cardiovascular pathophysiology through altered cellular transport balance, stress adaptation, and tissue homeostasis. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 27 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/59b155da-aa86-4cd3-9708-cecd5ee916b4.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=F99E1413CDCDE1C4)

To extend this pathway-level observation, the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis can be considered individually in relation to plausible heart failure mechanisms. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, NOS3 is one of the strongest candidates for relevance to heart failure because endothelial dysfunction, impaired angiogenesis, abnormal vascular permeability, and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability are central mechanisms in both chronic heart failure and cardiac remodeling. The described function indicates a key upstream role in vascular endothelial growth factor dependent endothelial signaling, including mitogen-activated protein kinase, protein kinase B, focal adhesion kinase, and nitric oxide pathways, all of which are highly relevant to myocardial perfusion, microvascular integrity, and adaptive vascular responses under hemodynamic stress. In heart failure, defective endothelial signaling can worsen tissue hypoxia, impair cardiac capillary maintenance, and promote inflammation and fibrosis. The noted regulation of actin cytoskeleton remodeling and endothelial migration further links this protein to vascular repair and remodeling processes that influence progression of ischemic and non-ischemic heart failure.

Along the same endothelial and vascular axis, THBD also appears potentially important in this context. THBD stands out because heart failure is increasingly recognized as a syndrome involving endothelial injury, thromboinflammation, and microvascular dysfunction in addition to impaired pump performance. The protein’s anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory functions are especially pertinent: by promoting activated protein C generation, modulating thrombin signaling, reducing endothelial permeability, and neutralizing high mobility group box 1 driven inflammation, THBD may counteract several pathophysiologic processes that exacerbate heart failure, including vascular inflammation, capillary leak, maladaptive coagulation, and end-organ congestion. Its role in angiogenesis further strengthens its relevance, as impaired vascular homeostasis contributes to myocardial ischemia, fibrosis, and progressive ventricular dysfunction. Thus, THBD represents a mechanistically important endothelial protective factor in the context of heart failure biology.[PubMed:38174561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38174561) 

Shifting from vascular protection to structural remodeling, TFPI2 may be relevant through extracellular matrix regulation. TFPI2 is potentially relevant to heart failure because extracellular matrix turnover is a major determinant of ventricular remodeling, chamber stiffness, and fibrosis. Its reported ability to regulate plasmin-mediated matrix remodeling suggests a role in controlling proteolytic degradation of the extracellular matrix, a process that is tightly linked to post-injury remodeling and progression to systolic or diastolic dysfunction. In addition, inhibition of factor sevena and tissue factor connects TFPI2 to coagulation-associated inflammatory signaling, which is increasingly implicated in heart failure pathogenesis. Although TFPI2 is less directly established than endothelial signaling proteins, it is noteworthy because dysregulated matrix remodeling is a hallmark of adverse cardiac remodeling after pressure overload, ischemia, or chronic inflammation.

This remodeling theme continues with TGFBR3, which may connect more directly to profibrotic signaling. TGFBR3 is highly relevant to heart failure because transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway dysregulation is central to cardiac fibrosis, fibroblast activation, vascular remodeling, and maladaptive structural changes in the failing heart. The described functions indicate that TGFBR3 modulates ligand availability and receptor trafficking, thereby influencing downstream signaling intensity and cellular responses. Its effects on migration, cytoskeletal organization, adhesion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transformation-like programs are particularly important because analogous mesenchymal activation pathways contribute to fibro-inflammatory remodeling in the myocardium and vasculature. Through these mechanisms, altered TGFBR3 activity could influence ventricular stiffness, extracellular matrix accumulation, and the transition from compensatory remodeling to overt heart failure.[PubMed:30364975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30364975) [PubMed:34910520](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34910520) 

At the level of cellular mechanics, ACTA2 may also fit within this broader remodeling framework. ACTA2 is of interest in heart failure primarily because it encodes smooth muscle alpha-actin, a core component of the contractile apparatus in vascular smooth muscle cells and activated myofibroblasts. Although the provided annotation is general, the actin cytoskeleton is directly relevant to vascular tone, arterial compliance, and fibrotic remodeling. In heart failure, increased vascular stiffness and fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition contribute to pressure overload, impaired relaxation, and ventricular fibrosis. Therefore, proteins governing cytoskeletal organization and contractile phenotype, such as ACTA2, may mark or mediate structural remodeling in both the myocardium and vasculature. Its importance is therefore mechanistic rather than disease-specific in the present annotation.

Beyond local tissue remodeling, several enriched proteins may reflect systemic stress responses that accompany more advanced disease. GDF15 is particularly interesting in heart failure because it is widely recognized as a stress-induced cytokine-like factor associated with systemic illness, cachexia, metabolic adaptation, and adverse prognosis in cardiovascular disease. The provided functional description emphasizes its induction by diverse stresses and its ability to trigger anorexia-related responses through glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor family receptor alpha-like and rearranged during transfection signaling in the brainstem. This is highly relevant to advanced heart failure, where chronic inflammatory and metabolic stress frequently lead to reduced appetite, weight loss, frailty, and cardiac cachexia. The noted effects on lipid metabolism also fit with the profound metabolic remodeling observed in heart failure. Thus, even though the annotation focuses on neuroendocrine stress signaling rather than direct cardiac action, GDF15 stands out as a biologically plausible mediator of systemic manifestations of heart failure and disease severity.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

A related but more cell-intrinsic aspect of heart failure biology involves energy metabolism, where ECHS1 may be relevant. ECHS1 is relevant to heart failure because the heart is highly dependent on mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, and impaired fatty acid oxidation is a well-established feature of failing myocardium. The described role of ECHS1 in beta-oxidation places it at the center of mitochondrial energy production, especially for short- and medium-chain fatty acid substrates. Energetic insufficiency, accumulation of toxic metabolic intermediates, and mitochondrial dysfunction all contribute to contractile impairment and adverse remodeling in heart failure. Therefore, alterations in ECHS1 function could plausibly exacerbate myocardial energetic stress, particularly in forms of heart failure linked to metabolic disease or inherited mitochondrial dysfunction.[PubMed:25125611](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25125611) [PubMed:26251176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26251176) 

Closely related to mitochondrial metabolism, GRPEL1 may contribute through maintenance of mitochondrial protein homeostasis. GRPEL1 is noteworthy because mitochondrial proteostasis is fundamental to cardiac function. Cardiomyocytes are densely packed with mitochondria and require efficient import of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins to sustain oxidative phosphorylation, redox balance, and stress adaptation. The described role of GRPEL1 in the presequence translocase-associated motor complex and mitochondrial heat shock protein 70 regulation suggests that it supports mitochondrial protein quality control and biogenesis. In heart failure, mitochondrial dysfunction is a central pathogenic mechanism, and defects in protein import can aggravate respiratory failure, reactive oxygen species accumulation, and energetic collapse. Thus, although GRPEL1 is not a classic heart failure marker, its function aligns strongly with a core disease mechanism.[PubMed:11311562](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11311562) 

In addition to mitochondrial stress, membrane lipid damage and lysosomal dysfunction are also increasingly implicated in cardiovascular disease, which brings PLA2G15 into consideration. PLA2G15 may have meaningful relevance to heart failure through its roles in membrane lipid remodeling, oxidized phospholipid detoxification, and lysosomal lipid metabolism. Oxidative stress is a major driver of cardiomyocyte injury and endothelial dysfunction in heart failure, and the ability of PLA2G15 to selectively hydrolyze truncated oxidized phospholipids suggests a potentially protective function against lipid-mediated cellular damage. Its contribution to bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate synthesis also implicates it in endolysosomal trafficking and cholesterol handling, processes increasingly linked to inflammation, autophagy, and metabolic dysfunction in cardiovascular disease. These functions make PLA2G15 an interesting candidate in the context of lipid stress and subcellular remodeling in failing hearts.[PubMed:10092508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10092508) [PubMed:11790796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790796) [PubMed:20410020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20410020) [PubMed:23958596](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23958596) [PubMed:25727495](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25727495) [PubMed:29724779](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29724779) [PubMed:30830753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830753) [PubMed:36823305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) 

Another major dimension of heart failure progression involves immune regulation, and LAIR1 may be relevant within that domain. LAIR1 is relevant because chronic low-grade inflammation and maladaptive immune activation are major contributors to heart failure progression. Its broad inhibitory effects on lymphocyte activation, cytokine release, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, and myeloid differentiation suggest that it could function as an endogenous brake on inflammatory pathways that otherwise promote myocardial injury, fibrosis, and adverse remodeling. In particular, suppression of interleukin 2, interferon gamma, interleukin 8, interleukin 10, and tumor necrosis factor related responses may influence the inflammatory milieu associated with both ischemic and non-ischemic heart failure. While the annotation does not directly mention cardiac tissue, the immunoregulatory profile of LAIR1 makes it biologically relevant to inflammatory mechanisms in heart failure.

Within the broader interface between inflammation and vascular injury, COLEC12 may also deserve attention. COLEC12 is potentially important in heart failure because oxidized low-density lipoprotein uptake, endothelial biology, and innate immune activation are all implicated in vascular dysfunction and atherosclerotic disease, which commonly underlie heart failure. The annotation specifically notes its role in recognition and degradation of oxidatively modified low-density lipoprotein by vascular endothelial cells, linking it to oxidative vascular injury and lipid-driven inflammation. Since endothelial dysfunction and chronic vascular inflammation contribute to reduced perfusion, increased afterload, and ischemic remodeling, COLEC12 may participate in upstream processes that predispose to or aggravate heart failure, particularly in cardiometabolic disease settings.

This inflammatory perspective is further supported by FCN1, which may connect innate immunity to disease exacerbation. FCN1 is of interest because innate immune activation and complement signaling are increasingly implicated in cardiac inflammation and heart failure progression. Its ability to activate the lectin complement pathway and stimulate monocytes to secrete interleukin 8 suggests a role in amplifying inflammatory responses. In heart failure, persistent activation of innate immunity can contribute to endothelial dysfunction, leukocyte recruitment, and myocardial remodeling. Therefore, FCN1 may be relevant particularly in inflammatory or infection-associated decompensation, even if its role is likely secondary compared with vascular and metabolic regulators.

Finally, CD99L2 may fit into this same inflammatory-remodeling continuum through its role in leukocyte trafficking. CD99L2 may be relevant to heart failure through its role in leukocyte trafficking across the endothelium. Leukocyte infiltration into the myocardium and vasculature is an important component of inflammatory cardiac remodeling, especially after ischemic injury and during chronic heart failure progression. By facilitating extravasation at the endothelial basement membrane, CD99L2 could influence the magnitude of immune cell recruitment into injured cardiac tissue. Although not a primary heart failure effector, it is mechanistically connected to inflammatory cell entry and tissue remodeling.

### endopeptidase activity (GO:0004175) 

Endopeptidase activity refers to the enzymatic cleavage of peptide bonds located within the interior of a polypeptide chain, rather than at the terminal ends. This catalytic function is executed by a broad and biologically diverse group of proteolytic enzymes, including serine endopeptidases, cysteine endopeptidases, aspartic endopeptidases, threonine endopeptidases, and metallopeptidases. In physiology, endopeptidase activity is essential for protein quality control, precursor protein processing, extracellular matrix turnover, signal peptide maturation, receptor activation, and the regulated degradation of structural and signaling proteins. Within the cardiovascular system, endopeptidases participate in myocardial tissue remodeling, inflammatory signaling, neurohormonal regulation, vascular homeostasis, and the turnover of contractile and cytoskeletal proteins. Because the heart depends on tightly controlled proteostasis and extracellular matrix integrity to preserve chamber geometry and contractile performance, both excessive and insufficient endopeptidase activity can have major pathological consequences. Dysregulated endopeptidase activity may promote degradation of matrix components, activation of latent cytokines and growth factors, cleavage of membrane receptors or ion handling proteins, and maladaptive remodeling of cardiomyocytes and the cardiac interstitium. Accordingly, this pathway is highly relevant to diseases characterized by chronic cardiac injury and remodeling, including heart failure.  

Building on this biological background, the potential connection between endopeptidase activity and heart failure can be considered in the broader context of established cardiovascular pathophysiology. Although no specific publications were provided for direct citation, the biological relationship between endopeptidase activity and heart failure is strongly supported by established cardiovascular pathophysiology. Heart failure is characterized by progressive structural remodeling, impaired contractile function, fibrosis, inflammation, and neurohormonal activation, all of which are influenced by endopeptidase-dependent proteolysis. Endopeptidases can contribute to degradation of extracellular matrix proteins, thereby altering myocardial stiffness, ventricular geometry, and chamber dilation; conversely, abnormal proteolytic processing can also facilitate fibrotic accumulation by modifying signaling pathways that regulate fibroblast activation and collagen turnover. In cardiomyocytes, excessive cleavage of sarcomeric, cytoskeletal, or calcium-handling proteins can impair force generation and excitation-contraction coupling, thereby worsening systolic and diastolic performance. Endopeptidase activity is also relevant to inflammatory and neurohormonal pathways because proteolytic processing can activate or inactivate cytokines, peptide mediators, and cell surface receptors that shape cardiac stress responses. Thus, in the setting of persistent hemodynamic overload, ischemic injury, metabolic stress, or inflammation, dysregulated endopeptidase activity may act as a mechanistic bridge between molecular injury and the clinical syndrome of heart failure by promoting maladaptive remodeling, loss of myocardial integrity, and progressive functional decline. However, because no pathway-specific publications were supplied here, this conclusion should be interpreted as a mechanism-based synthesis rather than a literature-specific evidence summary.

This mechanistic interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results obtained in the present analysis. There were 57 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of endopeptidase activity, indicating a substantial concentration of disease-relevant proteins within a proteolytic function that is central to myocardial remodeling, extracellular matrix turnover, inflammatory activation, receptor processing, and protein quality control. This protein count of 57 supports the biological importance of this pathway in heart failure, a condition characterized by persistent structural remodeling, impaired contractile performance, and progressive disruption of cardiac tissue homeostasis. Given that endopeptidase activity acts on peptide bonds within polypeptide chains and can influence both intracellular proteostasis and extracellular matrix integrity, the enrichment of as many as 57 proteins suggests that dysregulated proteolysis is not a marginal feature but rather a quantitatively prominent component of heart failure-related molecular pathology. We include the protein-protein interaction network visualization of these 57 proteins below, together with the link to the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes and Proteins webpage for interactive network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/6c33d6a5-b204-4823-a93d-2695f314c1af.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=78A69A99065EF49D)

To provide a more detailed interpretation of this enriched set of 57 proteins, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, PCSK9 has one of the clearest and most clinically meaningful connections to heart failure because it acts upstream of a major cardiovascular risk axis: lipid metabolism. By promoting degradation of LDLR and related receptors, PCSK9 increases circulating atherogenic lipoproteins, thereby contributing to coronary artery disease, ischemic myocardial injury, and subsequent ischemic heart failure. This is particularly important because a substantial proportion of heart failure arises as a downstream consequence of myocardial infarction and chronic ischemic remodeling. Beyond LDLR, the ability of PCSK9 to regulate VLDLR, LRP1, and LRP8 suggests broader effects on lipid uptake, cell survival signaling, and tissue homeostasis that may further influence cardiac remodeling. The translational importance of this protein is especially strong, as PCSK9 inhibition is already an established cardiovascular therapeutic strategy, making it highly relevant when prioritizing proteins with potential mechanistic or biomarker value in heart failure.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

From this lipid-centered mechanism, the discussion naturally extends to immune and inflammatory mediators that may also shape heart failure progression. CFD is highly relevant to heart failure because complement activation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to myocardial inflammation, adverse ventricular remodeling, endothelial injury, and progression of both ischemic and non-ischemic cardiac dysfunction. As an essential activator of the alternative complement pathway, CFD may amplify innate immune responses within the injured myocardium and vasculature. In heart failure, persistent low-grade inflammation and immune activation are important drivers of fibrosis, cardiomyocyte stress, and impaired cardiac function; therefore, proteins such as CFD that control complement propagation are mechanistically notable. Its role is especially compelling in settings of ischemia-reperfusion injury, microvascular dysfunction, and inflammatory remodeling, where excessive complement activity may worsen tissue damage and contribute to heart failure progression.

A related but distinct aspect of this pathway involves intracellular stress adaptation and antigen presentation. PDIA3 stands out because it bridges two processes that are highly relevant to heart failure pathobiology: endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis and adaptive immunity. Cardiac stress states, including pressure overload, ischemia, and metabolic injury, are characterized by protein misfolding, oxidative stress, and activation of unfolded protein response pathways. A disulfide isomerase such as PDIA3 may therefore influence cardiomyocyte survival and remodeling by regulating protein quality control under stress. In parallel, its essential role in major histocompatibility complex class one antigen presentation suggests a potential contribution to immune-mediated myocardial injury, particularly in inflammatory or post-viral forms of cardiomyopathy that can progress to heart failure. Although the provided annotation is not heart-specific, the convergence of proteostasis and immune activation makes PDIA3 a biologically plausible contributor to disease progression.

This interface between immunity and cardiac injury also brings attention to antiviral defense mechanisms. BST2 is potentially important in heart failure because viral infection and post-viral immune activation are recognized causes of myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy, both of which can culminate in heart failure. Its broad antiviral activity against diverse enveloped viruses, together with its role in interferon feedback regulation, makes it especially relevant to host defense mechanisms that may shape the severity and persistence of myocardial viral injury. Furthermore, its effects on nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling and matrix-remodeling-associated protease activity suggest additional relevance to inflammatory signaling and tissue remodeling, two central processes in heart failure progression. Thus, BST2 may be particularly informative in inflammatory, viral, or immune-mediated forms of cardiac dysfunction rather than in purely hemodynamic heart failure.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

In addition to antiviral and complement-related mechanisms, neutrophil-driven proteolysis may represent another inflammatory dimension of this pathway. PRTN3 is noteworthy in the context of heart failure because it links neutrophilic inflammation, extracellular matrix turnover, and endothelial interactions. These are all key processes in acute myocardial injury and chronic cardiac remodeling. By degrading structural matrix proteins, PRTN3 may contribute to tissue injury and remodeling after ischemic damage, while its role in neutrophil migration suggests relevance to inflammatory cell recruitment into injured myocardium and vasculature. Since excessive innate immune activation and maladaptive matrix remodeling promote ventricular dilation, fibrosis, and progressive pump dysfunction, PRTN3 represents a plausible mediator of inflammatory heart failure phenotypes. Its endothelial effects are also relevant because vascular dysfunction and leukocyte-endothelial interactions contribute to systemic inflammation and microvascular injury in heart failure.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Moving from inflammatory proteases to membrane-associated shedding events, ADAM9 may be relevant because its substrates and associated pathways intersect with angiogenesis, endothelial biology, inflammation, and cell-matrix communication. The cleavage of vascular regulators such as TEK, KDR, EPHB4, VCAM1, and CDH5 suggests that ADAM9 may influence endothelial integrity, vascular permeability, inflammatory adhesion, and reparative neovascular responses after myocardial injury. These mechanisms are important in ischemic remodeling and in the maintenance of myocardial perfusion and microvascular function. In addition, its ability to regulate cell motility and matrix interactions implies a possible role in fibroblast activation and tissue remodeling. Although the annotation is not cardiac-specific, ADAM9 stands out as a plausible modulator of the vascular and remodeling processes that shape heart failure progression.[PubMed:19273593](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19273593) [PubMed:9920899](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9920899) [PubMed:10825303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825303) 

Another mechanistic layer involves developmental and repair signaling pathways that are frequently reactivated in the injured heart. SFRP1 is particularly interesting because dysregulated Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is strongly implicated in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, vascular dysfunction, and repair after injury. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and lowering beta-catenin activity, SFRP1 may influence fibroblast behavior, vascular cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling pathways that are central to heart failure pathogenesis. Its reported antiproliferative effects on vascular cells and its ability to modulate angiogenesis further strengthen its relevance, as maladaptive vascular remodeling and impaired microvascular adaptation can worsen myocardial dysfunction. Therefore, SFRP1 may be important as a regulator of the balance between reparative and fibrotic responses in the failing heart.

In a similar signaling context, phosphoinositide three-kinase regulation may also be relevant to myocardial adaptation under stress. PIK3IP1 is relevant to heart failure because phosphoinositide three-kinase signaling is a major determinant of cardiomyocyte growth, survival, metabolism, and adaptation to stress. Even though the provided annotation emphasizes hepatic phosphoinositide three-kinase regulation, the biological pathway itself is highly central to cardiovascular disease. Negative regulation of phosphoinositide three-kinase may influence hypertrophic signaling, insulin responsiveness, and cellular survival programs that affect myocardial remodeling and heart failure susceptibility. This makes PIK3IP1 mechanistically interesting, particularly in metabolic heart failure phenotypes or in conditions where excessive or insufficient growth signaling contributes to disease progression. Its relevance is more pathway-based than directly demonstrated from the provided annotation, but the connection to heart failure biology is still meaningful.

Beyond signaling pathways, protease regulation within coagulation and inflammatory systems may also contribute to disease progression. AMBP merits attention because coagulation, thrombosis, and protease-driven inflammatory signaling are closely linked to heart failure progression. Its inhibition of factor ten a and prothrombin activation suggests possible relevance to thromboinflammatory pathways, which are important in atrial fibrillation-associated heart failure, venous congestion, and ischemic complications. In addition, inhibition of mast cell chymase may be particularly interesting, as chymase has been implicated in angiotensin two generation, fibrosis, and adverse cardiac remodeling. Thus, AMBP could theoretically influence both hemostatic and profibrotic mechanisms that contribute to worsening cardiac structure and function.

The extracellular matrix perspective can be extended further by considering proteins involved in hyaluronan organization. ITIH3 is potentially relevant to heart failure because hyaluronan is an important component of the extracellular matrix and contributes to tissue hydration, inflammation, and remodeling. In the failing heart, extracellular matrix reorganization is a defining feature that affects stiffness, fibrosis, and ventricular compliance. A protein involved in hyaluronan localization and turnover may therefore modulate the myocardial interstitial environment and influence the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive fibrosis. Although the evidence provided is indirect, ITIH3 stands out as a matrix-associated factor that could be relevant to structural remodeling in heart failure.

This remodeling-centered interpretation also connects with growth factor activation pathways. SPINT1 is of interest because it regulates protease systems linked to hepatocyte growth factor activation and epithelial or stromal remodeling. Hepatocyte growth factor signaling is broadly associated with tissue protection, angiogenesis, repair, and antifibrotic effects, all of which can be relevant in the injured heart. By inhibiting hepatocyte growth factor activator and related proteases, SPINT1 may indirectly influence regenerative and remodeling responses. Although the annotation does not directly establish a cardiac role, the connection to protease-controlled growth factor activation gives SPINT1 potential relevance in myocardial repair and fibrosis, especially after ischemic injury.[PubMed:9045658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9045658) [PubMed:28710277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28710277) [PubMed:20977675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20977675) 

Closely related to SPINT1, SPINT2 may be considered within the same reparative framework. SPINT2 is potentially relevant to heart failure because activation of hepatocyte growth factor and downstream mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling can influence tissue repair, cell survival, angiogenesis, and remodeling. Hepatocyte growth factor has been widely linked to cytoprotective and antifibrotic responses in injured organs, including the heart. Therefore, proteins regulating hepatocyte growth factor maturation may shape the myocardial response to injury and the progression toward adverse remodeling. Although the supplied annotation is not heart-specific and appears functionally broad, the hepatocyte growth factor-related aspect makes SPINT2 a plausible modulator of reparative signaling in heart failure contexts.[PubMed:20977675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20977675) [PubMed:28710277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28710277) [PubMed:34562451](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34562451)

### T cell modulation and desmoplasia in pancreatic cancer (WP:WP5078) 

T cell modulation and desmoplasia in pancreatic cancer describes a biological program in which malignant epithelial cells, cancer associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix components, myeloid cells, and T lymphocytes interact to produce a dense fibrotic and immunosuppressive tissue environment. Desmoplasia refers to the accumulation of activated fibroblasts, collagen rich extracellular matrix, matricellular proteins, and soluble mediators such as transforming growth factor beta, interleukin six, chemokines, and colony stimulating factors. In pancreatic cancer, this stromal reaction alters tissue mechanics, compresses blood vessels, restricts immune cell trafficking, and promotes persistent inflammatory signaling. T cell modulation within this setting includes impaired recruitment of cytotoxic T lymphocytes, enrichment of regulatory T lymphocytes, induction of T cell exhaustion, altered antigen presentation, and suppression by myeloid derived mediators and fibroblast derived signals. Although this pathway was originally defined in pancreatic cancer, its core biological themes are broader and include chronic inflammation, fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune cell polarization, and reciprocal communication between stromal cells and T lymphocytes. These same processes are highly relevant to nonmalignant fibrotic disorders, including heart failure, where immune activation and interstitial fibrosis are central determinants of ventricular remodeling and progressive dysfunction.

With this broader biological framing in mind, the relationship to heart failure can be considered through shared mechanisms of immune stromal interaction and fibrotic remodeling. No pathway specific publications were provided, so the relationship to heart failure must be inferred from the established biology embedded in the pathway description rather than from the supplied citation set. In heart failure, both reduced ejection fraction and preserved ejection fraction are characterized by persistent immune activation, expansion and phenotypic alteration of T lymphocyte populations, activation of resident and infiltrating fibroblasts, and excessive extracellular matrix deposition that produces myocardial stiffness, impaired relaxation, adverse chamber remodeling, and progressive decline in pump performance. The conceptual overlap with T cell modulation and desmoplasia in pancreatic cancer is therefore substantial: in both contexts, inflammatory cytokines and chemokines promote fibroblast activation; activated fibroblasts remodel the extracellular matrix and in turn shape immune cell recruitment and function; and sustained crosstalk between stromal cells and T lymphocytes amplifies a self reinforcing profibrotic state. In the failing heart, this biology is manifested as myocardial interstitial and perivascular fibrosis rather than tumor stroma, but the underlying logic is analogous. T lymphocytes can contribute to cardiac injury and remodeling through cytokine production and regulation of macrophage and fibroblast behavior, while fibroblasts and matrix derived signals influence immune cell retention and activation. Thus, the pancreatic cancer pathway is related to heart failure not because of a shared malignant origin, but because it captures a general disease module centered on immune stromal communication, fibrotic tissue remodeling, and chronic inflammatory persistence, all of which are fundamental mechanisms in heart failure pathogenesis. Because no relevant publications were supplied, direct citation based support specific to the provided pathway cannot be given.

This conceptual overlap is also reflected in the enrichment results derived from the heart failure associated protein set. There were 24 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of T cell modulation and desmoplasia in pancreatic cancer, a pathway that captures a biologically coherent program of chronic inflammation, fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune suppression, and stromal-immune crosstalk that is highly relevant to myocardial fibrosis and progressive ventricular dysfunction in heart failure. Although this pathway was originally defined in pancreatic cancer, its enrichment in a heart failure-associated protein set of 24 proteins supports the concept that shared multicellular processes, including transforming growth factor beta-driven fibrotic signaling, interleukin six-associated inflammatory activity, chemokine-mediated immune recruitment, altered T lymphocyte responses, and matrix accumulation, may contribute to disease progression across distinct tissue contexts. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 24 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/b64ac5a2-843d-45e0-abad-083acae324ed.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=FDCB24D99F8EEA6E)

Building on this enrichment pattern, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be especially relevant to the shared biology outlined above. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
VEGFA stands out as the protein with the clearest and most direct relevance to heart failure because impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal vascular permeability, and defective tissue perfusion are central features of cardiac remodeling and progression to pump failure. The described functions indicate that VEGFA signaling promotes endothelial survival and vascular growth while also stimulating nitric oxide production through NOS2/NOS3, an axis that is highly relevant to myocardial perfusion, coronary microvascular integrity, and afterload regulation. In the failing heart, inadequate capillary density and microvascular rarefaction can exacerbate ischemia, fibrosis, and adverse remodeling; therefore, a molecule that controls endothelial proliferation, migration, and survival has strong mechanistic relevance. Its ability to activate MAPK/ERK, AKT1, PI3K, FAK, and SRC signaling further links it to cell survival and stress adaptation pathways that are often dysregulated in heart failure. At the same time, excessive VEGFA-associated vascular permeability may also contribute to edema and maladaptive remodeling, suggesting a context-dependent role in disease progression. Overall, this protein is highly important because it connects vascular homeostasis, endothelial signaling, and tissue oxygen delivery, all of which are fundamental determinants of heart failure pathophysiology.

In parallel with vascular regulation, immune modulation emerges as another major theme in the enriched protein set. LGALS1 is particularly relevant to heart failure because it links immune regulation, apoptosis, and inflammatory cell programming, all of which are increasingly recognized as major drivers of cardiac remodeling. The listed functions show that LGALS1 can suppress immune activation by inducing T-cell apoptosis and restraining Th17 differentiation via CD69 activation, supported by the cited study. This is potentially important in heart failure, where persistent sterile inflammation contributes to fibrosis, ventricular dysfunction, and progression from compensatory remodeling to decompensated disease. Through its effects on apoptosis and cell differentiation, LGALS1 may influence not only immune-cell behavior but also tissue remodeling responses in the injured myocardium. Its inhibitory effect on CD45 phosphatase activity and downstream signaling modulation suggests a broader role in immune signal transduction, which could affect the inflammatory milieu in failing cardiac tissue. Thus, LGALS1 stands out as an immunoregulatory protein with plausible relevance to heart failure through control of maladaptive inflammation and remodeling-associated cell death.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Extending this immunological perspective, additional proteins in the enriched set may reflect adaptive immune pathways that shape myocardial injury and repair. TNFRSF9 is of interest in heart failure primarily because it reflects the growing importance of adaptive immune signaling in cardiac disease. Its role in promoting CD8-positive T-cell survival, cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial activity suggests that it may amplify immune responses in settings where inflammation contributes to myocardial injury, including viral myocarditis, post-infectious remodeling, and chronic inflammatory heart failure phenotypes. Enhanced CD8 T-cell persistence and function could be beneficial in viral clearance, but excessive or prolonged activation may also worsen myocardial damage and fibrosis, thereby contributing to ventricular dysfunction. The explicit connection to mitochondrial activity is also notable, since metabolic fitness of immune cells can shape the intensity and duration of inflammatory responses in the failing heart. Although the evidence provided here is indirect and based on similarity, TNFRSF9 remains a potentially meaningful immune checkpoint-like molecule in heart failure biology because it may modulate the balance between protective antiviral immunity and detrimental immune-mediated cardiac remodeling.

Finally, beyond immune signaling and vascular biology, extracellular matrix turnover provides another plausible point of convergence with heart failure remodeling. FAP may have a meaningful, although more indirect, connection to heart failure through regulation of protease activity and extracellular matrix turnover. By inhibiting plasmin and other proteases, FAP could influence fibrinolysis, proteolytic remodeling, and tissue repair processes that are central to post-injury cardiac remodeling. In heart failure, imbalanced extracellular matrix degradation and deposition contribute to fibrosis, chamber stiffening, and impaired systolic or diastolic function. Because plasmin participates in matrix remodeling and activation of downstream proteolytic cascades, a protease inhibitor such as FAP could affect scar formation and structural remodeling after myocardial injury. Although the functional description provided here is limited and does not directly mention cardiac tissue, protease regulation is mechanistically relevant to the remodeling processes that underlie heart failure progression.

### glycosaminoglycan binding (GO:0005539) 

Glycosaminoglycan binding refers to the selective and noncovalent interaction of proteins with glycosaminoglycans, which are long linear polysaccharides enriched in amino sugar residues and commonly present within the extracellular matrix and at the cell surface as components of proteoglycans. Major glycosaminoglycans include heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and hyaluronan. Through these interactions, glycosaminoglycans regulate the localization, stability, diffusion, and activity of many biologically important ligands, including growth factors, chemokines, cytokines, matricellular proteins, adhesion molecules, proteases, and protease inhibitors. Consequently, glycosaminoglycan binding is a fundamental mechanism controlling cell adhesion, leukocyte recruitment, inflammatory signaling, angiogenesis, fibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix assembly and turnover. In the cardiovascular system, these processes are highly relevant because myocardial homeostasis and injury responses depend on tightly coordinated communication between cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells, and the surrounding interstitial matrix. Altered glycosaminoglycan composition or altered glycosaminoglycan binding by signaling proteins can therefore reshape tissue remodeling responses after pressure overload, ischemic injury, or chronic neurohormonal stress.

Against this biological background, the relevance of this molecular function to heart failure can be considered in a cautious but mechanistically plausible manner. Although no specific publications were provided for direct citation, the pathway of glycosaminoglycan binding is plausibly and mechanistically linked to heart failure because heart failure is characterized by persistent extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation, fibrosis, vascular dysfunction, and maladaptive repair, all of which are strongly influenced by glycosaminoglycan-dependent molecular interactions. In the failing heart, the extracellular matrix is not merely a structural scaffold but an active signaling environment in which glycosaminoglycans bind and concentrate chemokines, growth factors, and profibrotic mediators, thereby controlling their retention, gradient formation, receptor access, and biological potency. These interactions can enhance leukocyte infiltration and sustain inflammatory activation, while also promoting fibroblast proliferation, myofibroblast differentiation, and excessive collagen deposition, which together increase myocardial stiffness and impair ventricular relaxation and contraction. Glycosaminoglycan binding also influences vascular permeability, endothelial signaling, and tissue edema, further contributing to adverse cardiac remodeling. In addition, proteoglycan-mediated sequestration or presentation of transforming growth factor beta family ligands and other remodeling cues may amplify fibrotic signaling pathways that are central to progression from compensatory hypertrophy to decompensated heart failure. Thus, even in the absence of pathway-specific publications in the provided material, the biological role of glycosaminoglycan binding supports its potential relevance to heart failure pathogenesis through integrated effects on inflammation, matrix remodeling, fibrosis, and impaired myocardial mechanics.

This conceptual framework is further supported by the enrichment results, which indicate that the signal is quantitatively substantial rather than isolated. There were 35 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of glycosaminoglycan binding, a molecular function defined by the selective and noncovalent interaction of proteins with glycosaminoglycans that are major structural and signaling components of the extracellular matrix and cell surface. This protein set size of 35 indicates a substantial functional module linked to extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory signaling, leukocyte recruitment, angiogenesis, fibroblast activation, and tissue remodeling, all of which are central biological processes in heart failure progression. In the context of heart failure, the enrichment of 35 proteins in this pathway supports the interpretation that altered glycosaminoglycan-dependent signaling is not a marginal event but instead represents a quantitatively meaningful component of disease biology, particularly because myocardial remodeling depends on coordinated communication among cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells, and the surrounding interstitial matrix. Given that glycosaminoglycans include heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and hyaluronan, the concentration of 35 disease-associated proteins within this functionally coherent category suggests that dysregulated ligand retention, diffusion, stability, and receptor accessibility may contribute materially to maladaptive remodeling after ischemic injury, pressure overload, or chronic neurohormonal stress.

To complement this enrichment summary, the interaction network below provides a structural view of how these 35 proteins may be functionally connected. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network visualization for these 35 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct inspection of the interaction structure and supporting evidence.
