Building on this network-level overview, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discusses their possible relevance in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
VEGFA is among the most directly relevant proteins to heart failure because myocardial homeostasis critically depends on adequate vascular supply, endothelial integrity, and adaptive angiogenesis. Impaired capillary density and endothelial dysfunction are well-recognized features of failing myocardium, whereas compensatory or maladaptive neovascular remodeling can influence ischemia, fibrosis, and ventricular performance. The listed functions place VEGFA at the center of these processes: it promotes endothelial survival and migration, increases vascular permeability, and activates AKT, ERK, FAK, and NOS signaling, all of which are highly relevant to myocardial perfusion and cardiac stress responses. In heart failure, altered VEGFA signaling may contribute either to insufficient vascular support of hypertrophied myocardium or to abnormal vascular leakage and remodeling. Its role in nitric oxide production is also notable, as nitric oxide signaling is a key determinant of vascular tone and endothelial-cardiac coupling.

In a related vascular and cardiomyocyte-protective context, FSTL1 appears particularly notable. FSTL1 stands out as a particularly compelling heart failure-related factor because its annotated functions include both vascular protection and direct cardiomyocyte survival. These dual actions are highly relevant to heart failure pathogenesis, in which endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory activation, and progressive cardiomyocyte loss jointly drive adverse remodeling. The ability of FSTL1 to support endothelial survival and angiogenic organization suggests a role in maintaining myocardial microvascular integrity, while its pro-survival effect on cardiac myocytes indicates a potential cardioprotective function during pressure overload, ischemic injury, or chronic remodeling. Its broader involvement in immune regulation further strengthens its relevance, since chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to heart failure progression.[PubMed:19595790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595790) [PubMed:21826198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21826198) [PubMed:20054002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20054002) 

Along similar lines, MDK may connect inflammatory control, tissue repair, and vascular adaptation after myocardial injury. MDK is highly relevant to heart failure because it integrates several core disease mechanisms: inflammation, tissue repair, angiogenesis, and cell survival. The annotation explicitly links MDK to the response after heart damage, where it limits inflammatory cell recruitment while promoting anti-apoptotic signaling and angiogenesis. This is important because heart failure often develops after myocardial injury and is shaped by the balance between reparative and maladaptive remodeling. Excessive inflammation can worsen fibrosis and ventricular dysfunction, whereas insufficient angiogenesis and cell survival accelerate cardiomyocyte loss. MDK therefore emerges as a multifunctional mediator that may influence post-injury remodeling, vascular adaptation, and myocardial preservation. Its signaling through MAPK and AKT further aligns it with canonical cardioprotective pathways implicated in stress adaptation and survival signaling in the failing heart.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

From vascular and injury-response mediators, the discussion naturally extends to transforming growth factor beta pathway components, which are often closely tied to fibrotic remodeling. TGFBR2 is one of the strongest mechanistic candidates for connection to heart failure because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central driver of cardiac fibrosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and maladaptive repair. The listed functions are directly aligned with pathological processes that underlie ventricular stiffening and progressive dysfunction, particularly extracellular matrix production, mesenchymal cell regulation, wound healing, and apoptosis. In the heart, overactivation of transforming growth factor beta pathways promotes fibroblast activation and collagen deposition, contributing to both systolic and diastolic dysfunction. The presence of both SMAD-dependent and non-canonical signaling routes is especially important, as these pathways can mediate distinct aspects of remodeling, including fibrosis, inflammation, and cell death. Thus, TGFBR2 is highly relevant to the structural remodeling that characterizes chronic heart failure.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

Closely related to this, TGFBR3 may further modulate the balance between fibrotic, inflammatory, and structural responses. TGFBR3 is relevant to heart failure because it modulates transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway activity, both of which are deeply involved in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, and vascular responses. Its effects on cell migration, adhesion, focal adhesion formation, and actin cytoskeleton organization suggest a role in tissue architecture and repair, while its ability to regulate nuclear factor kappa B links it to inflammatory signaling. Since heart failure progression depends not only on cardiomyocyte dysfunction but also on fibroblast activation, endothelial behavior, and inflammatory remodeling, TGFBR3 may influence multiple non-myocyte compartments of the diseased heart. Its participation in epithelial-to-mesenchymal-transition-like programs and RHOA-associated signaling also raises the possibility of involvement in fibrotic transformation and maladaptive structural remodeling.[PubMed:30364975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30364975) [PubMed:34910520](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34910520) 

Shifting from receptor-mediated remodeling signals to matricellular regulation, THBS2 may be relevant at the intersection of extracellular matrix turnover and angiogenic restraint. THBS2 is notable in the context of heart failure because extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenic balance are fundamental determinants of myocardial adaptation and decompensation. As a matricellular protein with antiangiogenic properties, THBS2 may restrain vascular growth in stressed myocardium, potentially contributing to capillary rarefaction and impaired oxygen delivery in hypertrophied or failing hearts. At the same time, its role in cell-matrix interactions suggests participation in fibrotic remodeling and altered mechanical properties of the myocardium. Antiangiogenic signaling through CD36 is particularly relevant because inadequate vascular compensation is a recognized feature of the transition from compensated hypertrophy to overt heart failure.

A related signaling axis involves Wnt pathway modulation, which has also been implicated in fibrotic and vascular remodeling. SFRP1 is relevant to heart failure because dysregulated Wnt/beta-catenin signaling has been implicated in cardiac fibrosis, hypertrophy, vascular remodeling, and repair after injury. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and lowering beta-catenin levels, SFRP1 may influence fibroblast activation, vascular cell behavior, and tissue remodeling within the failing heart. Its antiproliferative effects on vascular cells are also noteworthy, as vascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction are central features of chronic heart failure. Depending on context, SFRP1 could be protective by limiting maladaptive Wnt-driven fibrosis, or detrimental if it suppresses reparative angiogenesis or regenerative responses.

Another potentially relevant mediator of vascular adaptation is FGFBP1, which may connect growth factor activity with matrix-dependent signaling. FGFBP1 is potentially important in heart failure because fibroblast growth factor signaling contributes to vascular adaptation, tissue repair, and cellular survival under stress. The protein is particularly interesting because it links FGFR signaling with integrin engagement, thereby coordinating growth factor and matrix-dependent signaling. Its pro-angiogenic and pro-survival properties may be relevant to preserving myocardial perfusion and supporting reparative remodeling after injury. Activation of ERK1/2 also places FGFBP1 within signaling networks known to regulate hypertrophic growth and stress adaptation in cardiovascular tissues. Although its role in heart failure is likely context-dependent, its functions suggest a plausible contribution to myocardial vascular remodeling and survival signaling.[PubMed:8663044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [PubMed:28302677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [PubMed:1721615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [PubMed:3732516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [PubMed:3964259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [PubMed:23469107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [PubMed:29501879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

In addition to remodeling and angiogenesis, oxidative and inflammatory injury remains a major component of heart failure biology, which makes MPO noteworthy. MPO is highly relevant to heart failure through its strong connection to oxidative stress and inflammatory injury. Oxidative stress is a major component of heart failure pathophysiology, contributing to endothelial dysfunction, extracellular matrix remodeling, impaired nitric oxide bioavailability, and direct myocardial damage. MPO-derived oxidants can amplify inflammatory injury within the vasculature and myocardium, thereby promoting adverse remodeling and worsening cardiac function. The annotation also notes a potential compensatory vascular-protective effect through generation of t-alpha-1-microglobulin, but the dominant relevance of MPO in heart failure is its role as an inflammatory oxidant-generating enzyme. This makes MPO especially important in heart failure phenotypes associated with vascular inflammation, ischemia, and systemic immune activation.[PubMed:11593004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11593004) 

Returning to structural components of the extracellular matrix, VCAN appears relevant to ventricular stiffness and interstitial remodeling. VCAN is relevant to heart failure because extracellular matrix expansion and remodeling are core determinants of ventricular stiffness, fibrosis, and altered cell-matrix signaling. As a hyaluronan-binding proteoglycan, VCAN likely contributes to matrix organization, tissue hydration, and the mechanical properties of the interstitium. These processes are central to adverse remodeling in both systolic and diastolic heart failure. In addition, its role in regulating cell motility and differentiation suggests that VCAN may influence fibroblast behavior, inflammatory cell trafficking, and reparative remodeling after cardiac injury. Even though the annotation is broad, the matrix-centered functions make VCAN a plausible contributor to fibrotic and structural aspects of heart failure.

Within the same structural remodeling theme, PRELP may be of interest because matrix anchoring and basement membrane stability can influence myocardial mechanics. PRELP is of interest in heart failure because basement membrane integrity and extracellular matrix organization are important for myocardial structure, capillary stability, and mechanotransduction. Although its annotation is concise, proteins that stabilize matrix architecture can influence ventricular compliance and the quality of tissue repair after injury. In the setting of heart failure, abnormal matrix anchoring and remodeling may contribute to fibrosis, microvascular dysfunction, and altered force transmission across the myocardial interstitium. PRELP therefore represents a potentially relevant extracellular matrix component in structural remodeling.

Extending this extracellular matrix perspective to proteolytic remodeling, CLEC3B may also warrant consideration. CLEC3B is potentially relevant to heart failure because plasminogen-related pathways intersect with extracellular matrix turnover, fibrinolysis, and tissue remodeling. In failing hearts, the balance between matrix deposition and degradation is a major determinant of fibrosis and ventricular geometry. By binding plasminogen, CLEC3B may influence proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular environment, which could affect scar maturation, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling. Although the annotation does not directly mention cardiac biology, this matrix-remodeling connection makes CLEC3B a plausible protein of interest in heart failure-related tissue remodeling.

Another matricellular regulator that may fit within this remodeling framework is CCN3. CCN3 is relevant to heart failure because it belongs to a matricellular signaling family often implicated in tissue remodeling, fibrosis, and vascular adaptation. Its ability to regulate differentiation, apoptosis, and especially angiogenesis makes it potentially important in the remodeling myocardium, where endothelial growth and stromal signaling strongly influence disease progression. The fact that CCN3 negatively regulates endothelial proliferation and sprouting suggests that it could limit adaptive neovascularization in stressed cardiac tissue. In parallel, its broad effects on cell fate and mesenchymal programs may influence fibroblast behavior and reparative responses. Thus, CCN3 may contribute to the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive remodeling in heart failure.

Finally, SMOC2 may be considered a candidate of interest because it appears to combine matrix-regulatory and vascular effects within a single protein. SMOC2 is a notable candidate for heart failure relevance because it combines matrix-regulatory and pro-angiogenic functions. Both processes are central to the failing heart, where extracellular matrix remodeling alters ventricular stiffness and geometry, and impaired microvascular adaptation contributes to progressive dysfunction. By promoting matrix assembly, SMOC2 may influence fibrotic architecture and mechanical remodeling, while its stimulation of endothelial proliferation and migration suggests a role in vascular repair or neovascularization. This dual activity makes SMOC2 particularly interesting in the context of post-injury remodeling and chronic myocardial stress.

### Regulation of Insulin-like Growth Factor transport and uptake by Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Proteins (REAC:R-HSA-381426) 

Regulation of insulin-like growth factor transport and uptake by insulin-like growth factor binding proteins is a pathway that governs the bioavailability, tissue distribution, receptor access, and local actions of insulin-like growth factors. Insulin-like growth factor one and insulin-like growth factor two are peptide growth factors with major roles in cellular growth, survival, metabolism, differentiation, and tissue repair. In the circulation and in the extracellular space, these ligands are not freely available in large amounts because they are bound by a family of insulin-like growth factor binding proteins. These binding proteins function as transport carriers, prolong ligand half-life, restrict or facilitate movement across vascular and interstitial compartments, and regulate the fraction of ligand that can engage the insulin-like growth factor one receptor or related receptors at the cell surface. Their actions are further modified by proteases that cleave insulin-like growth factor binding proteins, by extracellular matrix interactions that sequester binding proteins and growth factors in tissue niches, and by changes in expression induced by hormones, nutrient status, inflammation, hypoxia, and mechanical stress. As a result, this pathway is not a simple buffering system, but rather a dynamic regulatory network that may determine whether insulin-like growth factor signaling promotes anabolic growth, cytoprotection, regeneration, or maladaptive remodeling in a given tissue. In the heart, insulin-like growth factor signaling has been linked to cardiomyocyte survival, contractile adaptation, mitochondrial function, vascular support, and responses to injury, while insulin-like growth factor binding proteins may either preserve controlled ligand delivery or limit receptor activation depending on context.

Against this biological background, the potential relevance of the pathway to heart failure becomes more apparent. Although no relevant publications were provided in the input list, the pathway is biologically plausible and highly relevant to heart failure because heart failure develops through a combination of cardiomyocyte loss, impaired energetic homeostasis, fibrosis, inflammation, microvascular dysfunction, and maladaptive remodeling, all of which intersect with insulin-like growth factor biology. In general, insulin-like growth factor one signaling in the myocardium is considered pro-survival and reparative, as it can support cardiomyocyte viability, reduce apoptosis, improve metabolic efficiency, and contribute to adaptive growth and vascular maintenance. Consequently, regulation of transport and uptake by insulin-like growth factor binding proteins would be expected to influence the intensity, duration, and localization of these protective signals. Increased sequestration of insulin-like growth factors by binding proteins may reduce receptor engagement and thereby weaken endogenous repair responses, whereas controlled release of ligand through binding protein proteolysis or altered extracellular matrix binding may enhance local signaling after injury. At the same time, persistent or unbalanced activation of growth factor pathways can also contribute to pathological hypertrophy and remodeling, indicating that the net effect of this pathway in heart failure is context dependent rather than uniformly beneficial. In patients with heart failure, systemic metabolic disturbance, neurohormonal activation, renal dysfunction, inflammation, and cachexia can all alter concentrations of insulin-like growth factors and insulin-like growth factor binding proteins, potentially shifting the pathway toward reduced anabolic support and impaired tissue resilience. Therefore, this pathway is best understood as a regulatory axis that may modulate whether insulin-like growth factor actions in the failing heart remain adaptive and cytoprotective or become insufficient to counter progressive myocardial dysfunction. Because no publications were supplied, this conclusion should be regarded as a mechanistic synthesis rather than a literature-supported pathway-specific evidence summary.

This mechanistic interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results observed in the present dataset. There were 35 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway Regulation of insulin-like growth factor transport and uptake by insulin-like growth factor binding proteins. This pathway describes a quantitatively important extracellular regulatory system that controls the availability, tissue distribution, receptor accessibility, and local biological activity of insulin-like growth factor one and insulin-like growth factor two, thereby shaping cellular growth, survival, metabolism, differentiation, and tissue repair. In the context of heart failure, the enrichment of 35 proteins in this pathway supports a strong functional connection between altered insulin-like growth factor handling and disease biology, because the pathway integrates ligand sequestration, transport, proteolytic release, extracellular matrix retention, and context-dependent receptor activation. These regulatory layers are especially relevant to the failing heart, where cardiomyocyte survival, contractile adaptation, mitochondrial performance, vascular support, injury responses, and maladaptive remodeling are all influenced by the balance between preserved insulin-like growth factor signaling and excessive restriction of ligand access. The presence of 35 enriched proteins indicates that this is not a marginal signal within the dataset, but rather a substantial pathway-level convergence that is consistent with broad remodeling of growth factor regulation in heart failure.

Building on this network-level view, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be particularly relevant to heart failure biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

FSTL1 is among the most compelling proteins in this list in relation to heart failure because its annotated functions directly converge on two central determinants of cardiac decompensation: cardiomyocyte survival and vascular adaptation. Heart failure is characterized by progressive myocyte loss, maladaptive remodeling, impaired tissue perfusion, and inflammatory activation. The reported ability of FSTL1 to promote endothelial cell survival and angiogenic network formation, together with its pro-survival activity in cardiac myocytes, suggests a potentially protective role in preserving myocardial viability and supporting compensatory vascular remodeling. Its capacity to signal through receptors linked to inflammatory and morphogenetic pathways further strengthens its relevance, as dysregulated immune signaling and aberrant repair responses are major drivers of heart failure progression. Accordingly, FSTL1 stands out as a plausible mediator of myocardial stress responses and tissue repair, with functions that are mechanistically aligned with limiting ventricular remodeling and preserving cardiac function.[PubMed:19595790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595790) [PubMed:21826198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21826198) [PubMed:20054002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20054002) 

In a related but distinct way, GAS6 also appears relevant because it connects vascular biology with cell survival and thrombotic regulation. GAS6 is highly relevant to heart failure because it links vascular integrity, cell survival, and thrombosis, all of which are important in the pathobiology of failing hearts. Endothelial dysfunction and microvascular rarefaction contribute to myocardial ischemia, fibrosis, and impaired ventricular performance; therefore, a pathway that supports endothelial cell survival may influence disease progression. In parallel, the involvement of GAS6 in platelet activation and thrombotic regulation is notable, since heart failure is frequently accompanied by a prothrombotic state, vascular inflammation, and heightened risk of ischemic complications. Its broader effects on cell migration and survival also suggest a role in remodeling responses within the injured myocardium. For these reasons, GAS6 stands out as a multifunctional signaling molecule with potential relevance to both myocardial injury responses and the vascular complications that exacerbate heart failure.

The discussion then shifts from vascular and survival signaling toward extracellular matrix remodeling, another major feature of heart failure progression. TNC is particularly important in the context of heart failure because extracellular matrix remodeling is a defining feature of adverse ventricular remodeling. Although the annotation emphasizes developmental and neural functions, tenascin-C is fundamentally an extracellular matrix signaling protein that interacts with integrins and modulates cell migration and angiogenic behavior. In failing myocardium, matrix reorganization is tightly coupled to fibrosis, mechanical dysfunction, inflammation, and altered cell-matrix communication. A protein capable of influencing integrin signaling and endothelial sprouting is therefore highly relevant to the remodeling milieu that follows pressure overload, ischemic injury, or chronic myocardial stress. Its angiogenic activity may reflect a reparative component, whereas its matrix-regulatory properties may also contribute to maladaptive structural remodeling. Thus, TNC stands out as a strong candidate connecting extracellular matrix dynamics to heart failure progression.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

A closely related matrix-associated candidate is VCAN, which may further reinforce the importance of extracellular structural remodeling in the dataset. VCAN is relevant to heart failure because it represents a matrix-associated regulator of cell behavior, and extracellular matrix expansion and reorganization are central to myocardial remodeling. Through its ability to connect cells to the extracellular matrix and influence motility, growth, and differentiation, versican could affect fibroblast activation, inflammatory cell trafficking, and tissue stiffness, all of which shape the transition from compensatory hypertrophy to decompensated heart failure. Its interaction with hyaluronic acid further supports a role in matrix hydration and structural organization, processes that can influence ventricular compliance and interstitial remodeling. Although the annotation is broad, these functions are mechanistically compatible with fibrosis and adverse remodeling, making VCAN a meaningful protein of interest in heart failure-related tissue remodeling.

From extracellular matrix organization, the interpretation naturally extends to direct cell-cell coupling within the myocardium. CDH2 is noteworthy for heart failure because cell-cell adhesion is essential for coordinated tissue architecture and force transmission in mechanically active organs such as the heart. Although the supplied annotation emphasizes neural functions, the core molecular activity of N-cadherin as a calcium-dependent adhesion protein is directly relevant to cardiomyocyte coupling and tissue integrity. In heart failure, disruption of intercellular junctions contributes to impaired electromechanical coupling, maladaptive remodeling, and arrhythmogenic susceptibility. A protein whose primary role is to maintain stable homotypic adhesion therefore has clear conceptual relevance to the preservation of myocardial structure under stress. The cited evidence for adhesion-mediated regulation of cell behavior supports the broader interpretation that CDH2 may influence how cardiac cells respond to injury and remodeling signals.[PubMed:11433297](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11433297) [PubMed:17988630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17988630) [PubMed:25253890](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25253890) [PubMed:2762814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2762814) [PubMed:9655503](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9655503) [PubMed:24952463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24952463) [PubMed:26750727](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26750727) 

In parallel with these structural considerations, hemostatic and thromboinflammatory processes may also contribute materially to heart failure progression. FGA is highly pertinent to heart failure because coagulation, platelet activation, and tissue repair pathways are frequently activated in advanced cardiac disease. The formation of fibrin matrices is not only central to thrombosis but also to provisional wound healing scaffolds, inflammatory compartmentalization, and cellular migration. In heart failure, especially in ischemic or inflammatory settings, heightened thromboinflammatory activity can worsen microvascular dysfunction, promote embolic risk, and contribute to maladaptive remodeling. The annotation that FGA enhances SELP expression in activated platelets further underscores its connection to platelet-endothelial interactions, which are often perturbed in cardiovascular disease. Thus, FGA stands out as a protein linking hemostasis, inflammation, and tissue repair—three processes that materially influence heart failure progression and complications.

Consistent with this inflammatory dimension, immune regulatory mediators also emerge as plausible contributors within the enriched set. LGALS1 is relevant to heart failure because immune dysregulation and chronic inflammation are increasingly recognized as major contributors to myocardial remodeling and progression to pump failure. The annotated functions of galectin-1 indicate broad immunomodulatory activity, including effects on apoptosis and T-cell differentiation. These properties are important because inflammatory cell activation can drive fibrosis, myocyte dysfunction, and adverse remodeling, whereas altered immune checkpoint-like mechanisms may influence whether inflammation resolves or persists. Its ability to regulate apoptosis also raises the possibility of direct effects on cardiac or vascular cell survival in stressed tissues. Therefore, LGALS1 stands out as a plausible mediator at the intersection of inflammation, cell death, and remodeling in heart failure.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Beyond local myocardial remodeling, several proteins in the pathway may influence heart failure through systemic cardiovascular risk. PCSK9 is one of the most clinically relevant proteins in this list for heart failure, particularly because of its central role in lipid metabolism and cardiovascular risk. By promoting degradation of low-density lipoprotein receptor family members, PCSK9 increases circulating atherogenic lipoproteins and thereby contributes to coronary artery disease, a leading cause of ischemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure. This connection is especially important because myocardial infarction and chronic ischemia remain dominant pathways to ventricular dysfunction. Beyond lipid handling, the annotation suggests broader effects on receptor trafficking and sodium transport, which may have additional relevance to cardiovascular homeostasis. Consequently, PCSK9 stands out not necessarily as a direct mediator of myocardial remodeling, but as a major upstream determinant of the vascular disease burden that precipitates and worsens heart failure.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

A conceptually similar but more indirect link may be considered for APOA2. APOA2 is relevant to heart failure primarily through its role in lipoprotein biology and systemic cardiovascular risk. High-density lipoprotein metabolism is closely tied to reverse cholesterol transport, vascular inflammation, and endothelial function, all of which can influence the development of atherosclerotic disease and subsequent ischemic heart failure. Although APOA2 is not a classical heart failure effector, proteins that shape lipid handling may alter the long-term burden of coronary disease and myocardial injury. In addition, altered lipoprotein metabolism is common in metabolic syndromes that predispose to heart failure. Therefore, APOA2 is best viewed as an indirect but potentially meaningful contributor through pathways linking dyslipidemia and cardiovascular remodeling.

The interpretation can also be extended to systemic metabolic and cardiorenal factors that frequently modify heart failure severity. STC2 is potentially relevant to heart failure because calcium and phosphate balance are tightly connected to myocardial contractility, vascular calcification, and cardiorenal pathophysiology. Disturbances in mineral metabolism are common in chronic heart failure, especially in patients with concomitant kidney dysfunction, and can influence arrhythmia susceptibility, vascular stiffness, and disease severity. A protein involved in systemic calcium and phosphate homeostasis may therefore have indirect importance in shaping the metabolic environment in which heart failure develops or progresses. While the provided annotation is limited, the functional link to mineral handling makes STC2 a protein of interest, particularly in the broader context of cardiorenal and vascular complications.

Finally, the list includes another soluble regulator of growth factor signaling that may be relevant to remodeling and cachexia-related processes. FSTL3 is of interest in heart failure because transforming growth factor beta superfamily signaling is deeply involved in fibrosis, hypertrophy, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. By antagonizing activin- and bone morphogenetic protein-related pathways, FSTL3 may influence the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive remodeling in the stressed myocardium. In particular, signaling networks involving activins and myostatin-related molecules have been implicated in muscle mass regulation, cachexia, and structural remodeling, all of which are clinically relevant in advanced heart failure. Although the annotation does not directly mention cardiac tissue, the protein’s role as a soluble modulator of major growth factor pathways makes it a plausible regulator of systemic and myocardial remodeling responses.

### receptor complex (GO:0043235) 

A receptor complex is a molecular assembly composed of one or more proteins that binds an extracellular or intracellular signaling molecule and converts that binding event into a functional cellular response. In biological systems, receptor complexes serve as central organizers of signal detection, signal amplification, and signal specificity. They can be located at the plasma membrane, where they detect hormones, neurotransmitters, growth factors, cytokines, and pharmacological agents, or within the cell, where they respond to lipid-soluble ligands and other intracellular messengers. The functional properties of a receptor complex depend not only on the ligand-binding receptor itself, but also on associated co-receptors, adaptor proteins, scaffold proteins, ion channel subunits, kinases, phosphatases, and structural regulators that together determine ligand affinity, downstream signaling, desensitization, internalization, and transcriptional or metabolic outcomes. In the cardiovascular system, receptor complexes are essential for the regulation of myocardial contraction, relaxation, heart rate, vascular tone, inflammation, fibrosis, cellular survival, and neurohormonal adaptation. Because heart failure is driven by persistent neurohormonal activation, altered mechanical stress sensing, inflammatory signaling, and maladaptive remodeling, receptor complexes represent a broad mechanistic category through which disease-initiating and disease-perpetuating signals may be transmitted in cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells.

Against this biological background, the relevance of receptor complexes to heart failure can be interpreted at a systems level even when pathway-specific literature is not directly available. No pathway specific publication was provided, so a direct literature based attribution from the supplied references cannot be made. Nevertheless, in the context of heart failure, receptor complexes appear highly relevant because the disease is fundamentally characterized by abnormal activation and remodeling of signaling systems that act through receptor-containing molecular assemblies. Heart failure progression involves sustained stimulation by circulating and locally produced hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines, and stress-related mediators, all of which require receptor complexes to initiate changes in gene expression, calcium handling, contractile performance, metabolism, fibrosis, inflammation, and cell survival. Pathophysiologically, prolonged receptor complex signaling can initially support compensation by maintaining cardiac output and vascular perfusion, but chronic activation commonly becomes maladaptive, promoting ventricular hypertrophy, extracellular matrix accumulation, chamber dilation, arrhythmogenic instability, energetic inefficiency, and progressive loss of pump function. Conversely, impairment, desensitization, or altered composition of beneficial receptor complexes may reduce cardioprotective signaling and further worsen myocardial dysfunction. Thus, even without pathway-specific citations, the receptor complex category is conceptually and mechanistically linked to heart failure because it constitutes the immediate signaling interface through which neurohormonal stress and tissue injury are translated into the structural and functional remodeling that defines the syndrome. However, because the publication list is empty, this conclusion should be regarded as a general biological interpretation rather than a pathway-specific evidence synthesis from the provided literature.

This general interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results, which indicate substantial representation of heart failure-associated proteins within this functional category. There were 57 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of receptor complex. This enrichment is biologically consistent with the central role of receptor-mediated signal detection and signal transduction in heart failure, a disease characterized by sustained neurohormonal activation, altered mechanosensory signaling, inflammatory stimulation, fibrotic remodeling, vascular dysfunction, and impaired cellular survival responses. Given that receptor complexes integrate ligand recognition with downstream functional output across cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells, the identification of 57 proteins in this category suggests a broad and quantitatively substantial involvement of receptor-centered signaling machinery in heart failure pathobiology. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 57 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

To provide a more detailed interpretation of this enriched set, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified during the functional enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is highly relevant to heart failure because chronic innate immune activation and sterile or pathogen-associated inflammation are central drivers of adverse cardiac remodeling. Through its role in lipopolysaccharide sensing and downstream nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-dependent cytokine production, CD14 may amplify systemic and tissue inflammation, which is strongly implicated in myocardial dysfunction, endothelial activation, and progression of both acute and chronic heart failure. Its reported ability to respond not only to microbial ligands but also to electronegative low-density lipoprotein further strengthens its potential cardiovascular relevance, since modified lipoproteins contribute to vascular inflammation, atherosclerosis, and ischemic injury, which are major antecedents of heart failure. Thus, CD14 stands out as a plausible mechanistic link between infection-triggered inflammation, metabolic-vascular injury, and maladaptive cardiac remodeling.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

In a related inflammatory context, LY96 may further support the importance of innate immune receptor signaling in this protein set. LY96 is noteworthy in the context of heart failure because it is a key component of innate immune receptor signaling, best known as myeloid differentiation factor 2 in the toll-like receptor 4 pathway, which is centrally involved in inflammatory responses to danger signals and microbial products. Although the provided annotations emphasize responses to Toxoplasma proteins, the broader biological implication is that LY96 modulates macrophage and dendritic cell activation and cytokine balance. In heart failure, excessive innate immune signaling contributes to myocardial inflammation, fibrosis, endothelial dysfunction, and worsening ventricular performance, whereas compensatory anti-inflammatory pathways may influence disease resolution or chronicity. Therefore, LY96 may be relevant as a potential regulator of the inflammatory tone that shapes cardiac injury and remodeling.[PubMed:31226171](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31226171) [PubMed:33912181](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33912181) 

Moving from innate immune sensing to vascular injury, OLR1 appears especially notable because it connects inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms with ischemic heart disease. OLR1 is one of the strongest candidates for heart failure relevance in this protein set because it directly connects oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and atherosclerotic disease. These processes are central to ischemic cardiomyopathy and to the vascular abnormalities that worsen cardiac loading conditions and impair myocardial perfusion. By promoting nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation, reactive oxygen species production, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, leukocyte adhesion, and apoptosis, OLR1 may contribute to coronary artery disease progression and microvascular dysfunction, both of which can precipitate or aggravate heart failure. Its ability to recognize advanced glycation end products also suggests relevance to diabetic cardiovascular injury, another major substrate for heart failure development.

A complementary immune-remodeling perspective is provided by TREM2, which may influence how inflammatory cells respond during tissue injury and repair. TREM2 is potentially important in heart failure because macrophage activation, phagocytosis, and inflammatory resolution are critical determinants of post-injury cardiac remodeling. The annotations indicate that TREM2-TYROBP signaling controls myeloid cell activation, cytokine production, phagocytic responses, and cell survival. In the injured heart, these functions are highly relevant to clearance of dead cells, orchestration of inflammation, and transition toward either reparative fibrosis or persistent inflammatory damage. The dual activating and inhibitory properties of this pathway are especially interesting, as heart failure progression often depends on the balance between effective tissue repair and sustained innate immune activation. Thus, TREM2 stands out as a candidate regulator of immune cell behavior in myocardial injury and remodeling.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

In addition to inflammatory pathways, several proteins in the enriched set may be linked to repair, proliferation, and structural remodeling. FGFR2 is relevant to heart failure primarily because pathways controlling cell proliferation, differentiation, and wound healing often become reactivated during cardiac stress and remodeling. Although the provided annotation is broad and not heart-specific, fibroblast growth factor signaling has recognized importance in tissue repair, fibrosis, angiogenesis, and structural remodeling after injury. In the failing heart, dysregulated reparative signaling can contribute either to adaptive healing or to maladaptive fibrosis and chamber remodeling. Therefore, FGFR2 deserves attention as a potential mediator of repair-associated signaling programs that may influence myocardial remodeling and progression to heart failure.

Along similar lines, systemic mineral regulation may intersect with myocardial biology through receptor-mediated signaling. PTH1R may have a meaningful connection to heart failure through systemic calcium and mineral metabolism, which are increasingly recognized as contributors to cardiovascular remodeling and cardiorenal disease. Disturbances in parathyroid hormone signaling are common in chronic kidney disease and advanced heart failure, where altered calcium-phosphate homeostasis, vascular calcification, and neurohormonal dysregulation can worsen outcomes. Although the annotation provided is not directly cardiac, the receptor's central role in calcium regulation makes it biologically relevant, particularly given the importance of calcium handling in myocardial contractility and the strong association between mineral metabolism disorders and heart failure progression.

This intersection between inflammation, calcification, and remodeling is also reflected in TNFRSF11B-related signaling. TNFRSF11B-related signaling is potentially relevant to heart failure because it integrates inflammation, calcium signaling, and reactive oxygen species generation, three processes that are central to cardiovascular remodeling. The annotation highlights its ability to influence dendritic cell and T cell interactions, suggesting broader immunoregulatory functions beyond bone biology. In heart failure, immune cell activation and oxidative stress contribute to fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and progressive contractile dysfunction. Moreover, the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells ligand, and osteoprotegerin axis has been linked in cardiovascular research to vascular calcification and inflammatory remodeling. Thus, this pathway stands out as a plausible interface between immune activation, oxidative stress, and systemic remodeling processes relevant to heart failure.[PubMed:22664871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664871) 

Whereas several of the preceding proteins are associated with inflammatory activation, GPR37 may be more relevant to inflammatory resolution and tissue repair. GPR37 is of interest for heart failure because its annotated functions point to a role in inflammatory resolution rather than simple immune activation. It promotes macrophage phagocytosis, shifts cytokine release toward an anti-inflammatory profile, and enhances efferocytosis, all of which are highly relevant to tissue repair after injury. In the heart, efficient clearance of apoptotic cells and timely resolution of inflammation are essential for limiting infarct expansion, preventing chronic inflammatory remodeling, and preserving ventricular function. Although the provided data derive largely from macrophage and nervous system contexts, the underlying biology suggests that GPR37 could mark or regulate reparative immune programs that may be beneficial in heart failure, especially after ischemic or inflammatory cardiac injury.[PubMed:26961174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26961174) [PubMed:28642167](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28642167) [PubMed:30010619](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30010619) [PubMed:34678058](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34678058) [PubMed:33731716](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33731716) [PubMed:37436891](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37436891) 

Beyond immune and reparative programs, metabolic regulation may also contribute to the relevance of this receptor complex-associated set. PTPRN2 may be relevant to heart failure through metabolic and secretory mechanisms. Its role in insulin vesicle accumulation and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion suggests a connection to systemic metabolic control, and metabolic dysfunction is a major driver of heart failure susceptibility and progression, particularly in diabetic cardiomyopathy. In addition, regulation of phosphoinositide signaling and actin dynamics may affect broader cellular secretory and structural processes. While the annotation does not directly implicate the heart, the links to endocrine function, glucose homeostasis, and membrane signaling make PTPRN2 a potentially informative candidate in heart failure settings characterized by insulin resistance, diabetes, or neurohormonal dysregulation.[PubMed:21732083](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21732083) [PubMed:15220191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220191) [PubMed:16418280](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16418280) [PubMed:16269463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16269463) [PubMed:19019914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19019914) [PubMed:12364328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12364328) 

Consistent with the broader theme of immune-cell communication, ALCAM may represent another interface between inflammation and cardiac remodeling. ALCAM is potentially relevant to heart failure because it combines two disease-relevant properties: immune cell costimulation and innate inflammatory sensing. By promoting T cell activation and immunological synapse maturation, ALCAM may contribute to adaptive immune responses that increasingly are recognized in chronic heart failure and post-injury remodeling. Its additional ability to bind bacterial products and trigger inflammatory signaling suggests a role in amplifying systemic inflammation, which can worsen myocardial dysfunction and endothelial activation. Cell adhesion molecules also influence leukocyte trafficking and tissue-level inflammatory organization, further supporting the plausibility of ALCAM as a contributor to inflammatory heart failure phenotypes.[PubMed:15048703](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15048703) [PubMed:15294938](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15294938) [PubMed:16352806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16352806) [PubMed:16914752](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16914752) [PubMed:24584089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24584089) [PubMed:24945728](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24945728) [PubMed:17601777](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17601777) 

Finally, ROR1 may connect developmental and inflammatory signaling pathways with mechanisms of remodeling that are relevant to heart failure progression. ROR1 is relevant to heart failure because noncanonical WNT signaling and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation are both implicated in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, and inflammatory signaling. The annotation specifically identifies WNT5A-ROR1 signaling as capable of activating nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, which is a major pathogenic pathway in myocardial stress responses. Although the strongest evidence here comes from developmental and oncogenic contexts, aberrant WNT pathway activation has been associated with fibroblast activation, hypertrophy, and tissue remodeling in cardiovascular disease. Therefore, ROR1 may represent a signaling node linking inflammatory and remodeling pathways that are mechanistically pertinent to heart failure progression.[PubMed:25029443](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25029443) [PubMed:27162350](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27162350) [PubMed:36949068](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36949068)

### humoral immune response (GO:0006959) 

Humoral immune response refers to the arm of immunity mediated through soluble factors present in body fluids, especially blood and lymph. It is classically driven by the activation of B lymphocytes and their differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells, but it also includes the coordinated actions of circulating complement proteins, cytokines, chemokines, acute phase reactants, and immune complexes. This pathway is initiated when antigens derived from pathogens, injured tissues, or altered self-structures are recognized by the immune system, leading to antigen presentation, helper T lymphocyte support, B lymphocyte activation, immunoglobulin class switching, affinity maturation, and the production of antigen-specific antibodies. The resulting soluble mediators can neutralize targets, opsonize particles for phagocytosis, activate complement cascades, and amplify inflammatory signaling across distant tissues. In addition to host defense, humoral immune response contributes to sterile inflammation, autoimmunity, and chronic tissue remodeling when directed against self-antigens or persistently activated by ongoing injury. In cardiovascular disease, these circulating immune mechanisms are increasingly recognized as important regulators of myocardial inflammation, extracellular matrix turnover, vascular dysfunction, and end-organ adaptation to hemodynamic stress.

Against this biological background, the potential relevance of this pathway to heart failure can be interpreted in a mechanistic framework, even though no directly matched publication set was provided for citation-based synthesis. In the context of heart failure, humoral immune response is biologically plausible as an important contributor because heart failure is accompanied by sustained tissue injury, neurohormonal activation, and systemic inflammation, all of which can stimulate circulating immune mediators. Myocardial stress and cell death may expose intracellular or modified cardiac antigens, thereby promoting antibody production and complement activation. These humoral processes can intensify myocardial inflammation, recruit additional immune cells, alter endothelial and microvascular function, and promote fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix remodeling, which together worsen ventricular stiffness, chamber dilation, and contractile dysfunction. Circulating cytokines and other soluble inflammatory mediators may also contribute to skeletal muscle wasting, renal dysfunction, and metabolic derangement, thereby linking cardiac injury to the broader multisystem manifestations of heart failure. In this way, dysregulated humoral immune response can be viewed not merely as a bystander phenomenon but as a potential mechanistic bridge between initial myocardial damage and progressive structural and functional deterioration. Because no pathway-specific publications were supplied, this relationship should be interpreted as a general mechanistic synthesis rather than a conclusion directly supported by the provided literature set.

From a quantitative perspective, the enrichment result further supports the relevance of this pathway within the analyzed dataset. There were 49 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of humoral immune response, indicating a quantitatively substantial immune-related signal within the analyzed protein set. This enrichment is biologically consistent with the central role of circulating immune mediators in myocardial inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular dysfunction, and systemic adaptation to hemodynamic stress in heart failure, particularly because this pathway encompasses antibody production, complement activation, cytokine signaling, chemokine regulation, immune complex formation, and soluble inflammatory amplification across tissues. Given that the enriched set contains 49 proteins, the result supports the interpretation that humoral immunity is not represented by an isolated signal but rather by a broad, multi-component functional module that may contribute to both protective host defense and maladaptive chronic inflammatory remodeling in the failing heart.

To complement this enrichment overview, the network-level organization of the 49 proteins provides an additional layer for interpretation. The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network for these 49 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the provided link for interactive exploration of network connectivity and functional relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/511b49a0-9233-462f-8e1f-3c978c94ce8c.png)
