Building on this pathway and network context, the significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis can be considered individually in relation to heart failure biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CFD is highly relevant to heart failure because excessive activation of the complement cascade is increasingly recognized as a driver of sterile inflammation, endothelial injury, and adverse cardiac remodeling. By initiating activation of factor B on C3b, CFD promotes amplification of the alternative pathway, which can intensify myocardial inflammatory responses after tissue stress or injury. In the setting of heart failure, sustained complement activation may contribute to cardiomyocyte damage, microvascular dysfunction, and fibrotic remodeling, all of which worsen ventricular performance. Thus, CFD stands out as a mechanistically important inflammatory mediator with plausible relevance to progression of both ischemic and non-ischemic heart failure.

Closely related to this complement-centered theme, CFP may further sustain inflammatory amplification in heart failure. CFP is notable in the context of heart failure because it reinforces and prolongs complement activation, thereby potentially sustaining inflammatory tissue injury. Stabilization of C3 and C5 convertases can increase downstream generation of pro-inflammatory complement fragments and membrane attack activity, processes that may exacerbate endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, and myocardial injury. Since chronic low-grade inflammation and innate immune activation are central features of heart failure pathogenesis, CFP may contribute to maladaptive remodeling and worsening cardiac function by maintaining complement-mediated inflammatory signaling.[PubMed:28264884](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28264884) 

Extending this innate immune framework, FCN1 may link immune sensing with downstream inflammatory recruitment. FCN1 is potentially important for heart failure because it links innate immune sensing to complement activation and monocyte-driven inflammation. Heart failure is increasingly understood as a syndrome shaped by persistent activation of innate immunity, even in the absence of overt infection. Through lectin-pathway complement activation and induction of IL-8, FCN1 may promote inflammatory cell recruitment, endothelial perturbation, and tissue remodeling. These mechanisms are especially relevant in heart failure phenotypes associated with systemic inflammation, vascular dysfunction, and post-injury remodeling.

In parallel with complement biology, coagulation-related mechanisms may also intersect with heart failure progression. FGA is among the most compelling proteins in relation to heart failure because coagulation, thrombosis, and inflammation are deeply intertwined with cardiac decompensation. Fibrin formation contributes to hemostasis, but excessive fibrinogen/fibrin activity can also reflect and promote a prothrombotic, pro-inflammatory state that is common in heart failure. Fibrin deposition may influence microvascular perfusion, endothelial function, and tissue repair responses, while platelet activation and immune modulation may further aggravate vascular and myocardial injury. Elevated fibrinogen-related pathways are therefore biologically plausible contributors to adverse remodeling, congestion-associated vascular complications, and thromboembolic risk in heart failure.

Shifting from complement and coagulation to immune surveillance, HLA-E may be of interest particularly in infection-associated cardiac stress states. HLA-E is particularly relevant to heart failure in the setting of viral infection, especially coronavirus disease 2019-associated cardiovascular complications. Viral-triggered immune dysregulation can precipitate myocarditis, worsen pre-existing heart failure, and promote systemic inflammation that destabilizes cardiac function. The reported ability of HLA-E to contribute to natural killer cell and cluster of differentiation 8 positive T-cell exhaustion suggests a mechanism by which antiviral control becomes impaired, potentially prolonging inflammatory injury. This is clinically meaningful because viral infections are established precipitants of acute heart failure exacerbation and may also contribute to longer-term myocardial dysfunction.[PubMed:32859121](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32859121) 

A related cytotoxic immune axis is reflected by NCR3LG1, which may influence inflammatory communication between immune cell populations. NCR3LG1 is relevant to heart failure because it sits at the interface of cytotoxic immunity and inflammatory cytokine production. Natural killer cell activation and release of tumor necrosis factor alpha and interferon gamma may influence myocardial inflammation, endothelial activation, and remodeling. Inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha have long been implicated in heart failure progression, contributing to cardiomyocyte dysfunction, cachexia, and maladaptive remodeling. Therefore, proteins that shape natural killer cell and dendritic cell crosstalk, such as NCR3LG1, may have indirect but meaningful relevance to inflammatory heart failure phenotypes.

In addition to immune signaling, tissue-destructive protease activity may also contribute to structural remodeling. PRTN3 stands out because neutrophil activation, endothelial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix remodeling are all central to cardiovascular injury and heart failure progression. Its ability to degrade elastin, fibronectin, laminin, vitronectin, and collagens suggests a direct role in matrix turnover, which is highly relevant to ventricular remodeling and fibrosis. In addition, its effects on endothelial barrier biology and neutrophil transmigration indicate a role in vascular inflammation. These properties make PRTN3 a plausible mediator of inflammatory tissue damage in acute decompensation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and chronic remodeling states associated with heart failure.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Beyond inflammatory proteolysis, metabolic inflammation may represent another important layer of relevance. RARRES2 is highly relevant to heart failure because it integrates metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, vascular biology, and immune-cell recruitment—processes that are fundamental to modern heart failure pathophysiology, particularly in obesity-related and cardiometabolic heart failure. Its pro-inflammatory adipokine activity can worsen insulin resistance, lipid dysregulation, and vascular dysfunction, all of which increase cardiac stress. At the same time, its effects on leukocyte chemotaxis and endothelial activation suggest a role in systemic and local inflammatory remodeling. Because heart failure often emerges in the context of metabolic syndrome and chronic low-grade inflammation, RARRES2 is a particularly important candidate linking adipose dysfunction to cardiac disease progression.

At the post-translational level, glycosylation-related regulation may further shape inflammatory and remodeling responses. ST6GAL1 is noteworthy because protein sialylation can profoundly influence receptor stability, immune recognition, cell-cell interaction, and inflammatory signaling, all of which are relevant to heart failure. Altered glycosylation has been implicated in fibrosis, immune activation, and vascular dysfunction. As a central enzyme in terminal sialylation, ST6GAL1 may affect the behavior of circulating proteins, immune receptors, and endothelial or myocardial cell-surface molecules. Although its connection to heart failure is more indirect than that of complement or coagulation proteins, it represents a potentially important regulator of inflammatory and remodeling pathways.

Cell death signaling provides another mechanistic bridge between inflammation and cardiac dysfunction. TNFRSF21 is particularly compelling in heart failure because apoptosis, inflammatory signaling, and pyroptotic cell death are all strongly implicated in myocardial injury and adverse remodeling. Cardiomyocyte loss through apoptotic or inflammatory cell death pathways contributes directly to progressive contractile dysfunction. In parallel, TNFRSF21-mediated regulation of T-cell activity and cytokine production may shape chronic immune activation, which is increasingly recognized in heart failure. Its reported link to reactive oxygen species-responsive pyroptosis is especially relevant, given the importance of oxidative stress in ischemic injury, pressure overload, and heart failure progression.[PubMed:11485735](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11485735) [PubMed:11714751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11714751) [PubMed:12515813](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12515813) [PubMed:21725297](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21725297) [PubMed:23559013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23559013) 

Within the broader innate immune compartment, TREM2 may be relevant to the balance between injury resolution and persistent inflammation. TREM2 is relevant to heart failure because myeloid-cell activation and phagocytic remodeling are major determinants of post-injury repair and chronic cardiac inflammation. Although the provided annotations emphasize microglia and dendritic cells, the broader biology of the TREM2-TYROBP axis suggests a role in macrophage activation, tissue debris clearance, and inflammatory resolution versus persistence. In heart failure, especially after myocardial injury, these processes influence scar formation, fibrosis, and ventricular remodeling. TREM2 therefore stands out as a plausible immunoregulatory node connecting innate immune activation with structural progression of cardiac dysfunction.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

Moving toward more exploratory candidates, ANG-related biology may intersect with stress adaptation and vascular responses in heart failure. ANG-related biology may be meaningful for heart failure because stress adaptation, RNA metabolism, and angiogenesis are important determinants of myocardial survival under ischemic or hemodynamic stress. The described stress-responsive relocalization mechanism suggests a role in cellular adaptation to injury. Since impaired angiogenesis, oxidative stress, and maladaptive stress responses contribute to heart failure progression, proteins regulating ANG function may influence myocardial resilience, vascular remodeling, and tissue repair. This relevance is more exploratory than for complement or coagulation factors, but it is biologically plausible.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170) 

Finally, ROS1 may be considered as a tentative upstream signaling candidate within remodeling-related pathways. Although ROS1 is not a canonical heart failure protein, it is potentially relevant because the downstream pathways listed—phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B-mechanistic target of rapamycin, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3—are central regulators of cardiomyocyte growth, survival, metabolism, and hypertrophic remodeling. Dysregulation of these pathways can contribute to maladaptive hypertrophy, fibrosis, and progression to heart failure. Therefore, ROS1 may represent an upstream signaling node of interest, especially in contexts where aberrant growth-factor signaling or survival signaling influences cardiac remodeling.[PubMed:32499443](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32499443)

### external encapsulating structure (GO:0030312) 

The external encapsulating structure refers to the material located outside the plasma membrane that encloses a cell or a group of cells. In animal tissues, this concept is represented primarily by the extracellular matrix and associated surface-adherent structures, including basement membrane, interstitial matrix, and cell-surface glycocalyx-related assemblies that together provide mechanical support, spatial organization, and biochemical signaling cues. In the heart, the external encapsulating structure is essential for maintaining tissue architecture, coordinating force transmission between cardiomyocytes and the surrounding interstitium, regulating cell adhesion, and modulating communication among cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells. Its major components include collagens, fibronectin, laminins, proteoglycans, glycoproteins, and matrix-associated enzymes and inhibitors that collectively determine matrix composition, stiffness, and turnover. Dynamic remodeling of this extracellular environment is a central feature of cardiac adaptation and maladaptation, because changes in matrix deposition, degradation, and cross-linking influence ventricular compliance, chamber geometry, electrical coupling, capillary integrity, and inflammatory signaling. Thus, although the external encapsulating structure is not a single molecular pathway in the classical sense, it represents a biologically important structural and signaling framework that strongly influences cardiac homeostasis and disease progression.

Against this biological background, the potential relevance of this term to heart failure can be considered in a mechanistic manner, while remaining cautious about the evidentiary basis available here. No relevant publications were provided for direct citation-based analysis of this pathway in heart failure. On the basis of established biological knowledge, the relation between the external encapsulating structure and heart failure is likely to be substantial because pathological remodeling of the extracellular environment is a defining feature of failing myocardium. In heart failure, excessive deposition of collagen-rich matrix by activated cardiac fibroblasts, altered basement membrane composition, increased matrix cross-linking, and dysregulated matrix degradation can produce myocardial fibrosis, increased ventricular stiffness, impaired relaxation, and reduced mechanical efficiency. These changes also disturb cardiomyocyte alignment, impair electromechanical coupling, promote microvascular dysfunction, and sustain inflammatory and profibrotic signaling, thereby contributing to both progression of ventricular dysfunction and adverse remodeling after injury. Consequently, the external encapsulating structure should be understood as a key determinant of myocardial structural integrity and biomechanical behavior in heart failure. However, because no publications were supplied in the input, this assessment cannot be attributed to the requested source set and should be regarded as a general mechanistic interpretation rather than a publication-supported synthesis.

This general interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results, which indicate that proteins assigned to this compartment are prominently represented in the heart failure-associated set. There were 105 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the external encapsulating structure, indicating a substantial concentration of disease-related proteins within the extracellular material that surrounds and organizes cardiac cells. This enrichment is biologically notable because the external encapsulating structure in the heart comprises the extracellular matrix, basement membrane, interstitial matrix, and cell-surface associated assemblies that collectively regulate tissue architecture, mechanical stability, force transmission, cell adhesion, and intercellular signaling. In the context of heart failure, the identification of 105 proteins supports the interpretation that structural remodeling outside the plasma membrane is not a peripheral event but a major disease-associated process, consistent with the central role of altered matrix deposition, degradation, and cross-linking in determining ventricular stiffness, chamber geometry, capillary support, inflammatory signaling, and electrical coordination across the myocardium. The relatively large protein count further suggests that this enrichment captures a broad and integrated remodeling program involving collagens, laminins, fibronectin, proteoglycans, glycoproteins, matrix-associated enzymes, and their regulators, all of which are known to influence cardiac homeostasis and progression toward maladaptive remodeling.

To place these 105 proteins into a systems-level context, the interaction network provides an additional view of their potential biological connectivity. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 105 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection of the network relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/f7d4ca79-0387-414f-b680-d7ccd8457872.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=609DBBBA735A6969)

Building on this network-level overview, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified in the function enrichment analysis and considers, in a cautious manner, how their annotated functions may relate to heart failure biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

ANGPTL4 is highly relevant to heart failure because disordered lipid handling is a major component of cardiometabolic stress, particularly in obesity, diabetes, and ischemic heart disease, which are common antecedents of heart failure. By inhibiting LPL, ANGPTL4 can reduce triglyceride hydrolysis and alter fatty acid delivery to tissues, potentially reshaping myocardial substrate availability. In the failing heart, where metabolic flexibility is already impaired, regulators of circulating triglyceride clearance may influence lipotoxicity, systemic inflammation, and vascular dysfunction. Thus, ANGPTL4 stands out as a plausible link between extracardiac metabolic dysregulation and cardiac remodeling, especially in heart failure with metabolic syndrome features.[PubMed:19270337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19270337) [PubMed:21398697](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21398697) [PubMed:27929370](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27929370) [PubMed:29899144](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899144) 

In a related but distinct way, CCN3 points toward the interface between vascular adaptation and tissue remodeling. CCN3 is of interest in heart failure because it integrates developmental signaling, angiogenesis, and tissue differentiation, three processes central to myocardial remodeling. In the failing heart, maladaptive remodeling involves altered endothelial behavior, impaired microvascular support, fibroblast activation, and shifts in differentiation programs. The reported anti-angiogenic effects of CCN3 suggest that it could influence capillary rarefaction, a recognized contributor to myocardial dysfunction and progression to heart failure. Its broader roles in mesodermal development and cellular specification further support the possibility that CCN3 participates in structural remodeling and reparative responses after cardiac injury.

Extending this theme from vascular remodeling to immune-mediated tissue change, CHI3L1 appears particularly relevant. CHI3L1 is particularly noteworthy because heart failure is increasingly understood as a syndrome driven not only by hemodynamic stress but also by chronic inflammation and tissue remodeling. The described functions of CHI3L1 in remodeling, inflammatory cell regulation, macrophage polarization, and injury tolerance are directly relevant to cardiac fibrosis and adverse ventricular remodeling. Macrophage phenotype and inflammatory persistence are key determinants of post-injury healing and progression to chronic heart failure. Therefore, CHI3L1 may represent a mechanistic bridge between inflammatory activation and structural remodeling in the myocardium, especially in settings such as ischemic injury, pressure overload, or systemic inflammatory comorbidity.

A more direct connection to extracellular matrix accumulation is suggested by CTHRC1. CTHRC1 stands out because excessive extracellular matrix deposition and fibrosis are core pathological features of heart failure. Cardiac fibrosis increases ventricular stiffness, disrupts electrical conduction, impairs relaxation, and contributes to both systolic and diastolic dysfunction. A protein with the capacity to suppress collagen matrix accumulation is therefore highly relevant to disease progression and may influence the balance between adaptive scar formation and maladaptive interstitial fibrosis. In heart failure, especially heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and post-infarction remodeling, regulators of collagen deposition such as CTHRC1 may have substantial pathophysiological importance.

Closely aligned with matrix remodeling, EGFL7 shifts attention toward endothelial maintenance and vascular repair. EGFL7 is strongly connected to heart failure through its vascular functions. Endothelial integrity, angiogenesis, and vascular remodeling are critical determinants of myocardial perfusion and tissue repair after injury. By promoting endothelial adhesion and angiogenesis while restraining smooth muscle migration, EGFL7 may influence microvascular maintenance and pathological vascular remodeling. In heart failure, especially ischemic and hypertensive forms, impaired angiogenic compensation and endothelial dysfunction contribute to progressive myocardial hypoxia and fibrosis. EGFL7 therefore emerges as a candidate mediator of adaptive versus maladaptive vascular responses in the failing heart.

From the vasculature, the discussion naturally moves to basement membrane organization and structural integrity, where FLRT2 may be informative. FLRT2 is particularly compelling because its annotated functions directly mention cardiac basement membrane organization and heart morphogenesis. Although these roles are developmental, proteins governing basement membrane architecture and cell adhesion often remain relevant in adult tissue homeostasis and repair. In heart failure, disruption of myocardial extracellular matrix organization and altered cell-cell interactions contribute to ventricular dilation, reduced mechanical coupling, and impaired reparative remodeling. FLRT2 may therefore have relevance not only to congenital susceptibility but also to structural integrity of the myocardium under chronic stress.[PubMed:21350012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21350012) [PubMed:25374360](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25374360) [PubMed:25728924](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25728924) [PubMed:21673655](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21673655) [PubMed:16872596](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16872596) 

Immune regulation remains another major dimension of remodeling, and LGALS1 may be relevant within this context. LGALS1 is relevant to heart failure because immune dysregulation and chronic low-grade inflammation are central features of disease progression. Through effects on apoptosis and T-cell differentiation, LGALS1 may influence the inflammatory milieu that drives ventricular remodeling and fibrosis. Its capacity to modulate adaptive immunity is especially important in nonischemic cardiomyopathies, myocarditis-related remodeling, and chronic heart failure states characterized by persistent immune activation. By affecting both cell survival and inflammatory polarization, LGALS1 may contribute to the balance between injury resolution and maladaptive remodeling.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

At the level of growth factor control, LRIG1 may represent a modulatory component of stress signaling. LRIG1 is important in the context of heart failure because receptor tyrosine kinase pathways regulate cardiomyocyte survival, hypertrophic signaling, fibroblast activation, and vascular responses. A negative regulator of these pathways may shape the amplitude and duration of growth factor signaling during cardiac stress. Excessive or prolonged receptor tyrosine kinase signaling can drive maladaptive hypertrophy and fibrosis, whereas insufficient signaling may impair repair and cell survival. Accordingly, LRIG1 may be relevant as a homeostatic modulator of remodeling pathways in the injured or failing heart.

Among the proteins listed, MDK appears especially notable because its annotated functions span several processes that are central to injury response. MDK is one of the strongest candidates for relevance to heart failure in this list because its annotated functions directly encompass post-injury inflammation, angiogenesis, tissue regeneration, and cardioprotective signaling. The description specifically notes that after heart damage MDK can reduce inflammatory cell recruitment and promote cell survival through anti-apoptotic MAPK and AKT signaling, while also supporting angiogenesis. These mechanisms are central to limiting infarct expansion, preserving viable myocardium, and improving remodeling after injury. At the same time, MDK has broad effects on immune activation and cell migration, indicating that its impact may be context dependent, potentially protective in acute repair but maladaptive if chronically dysregulated. This duality is highly characteristic of heart failure biology.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Whereas MDK may support repair in some contexts, PRTN3 highlights the possibility of inflammatory proteolysis contributing to tissue injury. PRTN3 is relevant to heart failure because extracellular matrix degradation, endothelial dysfunction, and neutrophil-driven inflammation are all major components of acute cardiac injury and chronic remodeling. By degrading elastin, fibronectin, laminin, vitronectin, and collagens, PRTN3 may contribute to matrix turnover and tissue injury. Its involvement in neutrophil transmigration and inflammatory activation further links it to sterile inflammation after myocardial infarction or pressure overload. Since excessive inflammatory protease activity can amplify ventricular remodeling and impair vascular integrity, PRTN3 may participate in the transition from acute injury to chronic heart failure.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

A broader systemic connection between adipose biology, inflammation, and vascular function is suggested by RARRES2. RARRES2 is highly pertinent to heart failure because it links adipose tissue dysfunction, systemic inflammation, endothelial biology, and metabolic disease. These processes are particularly important in obesity-associated heart failure and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, where adipose inflammation and vascular dysfunction are prominent. The ability of RARRES2 to modulate leukocyte recruitment, adipocyte differentiation, insulin sensitivity, and endothelial activation suggests that it may influence both systemic cardiometabolic burden and local vascular inflammation. Its reported anti-inflammatory endothelial effects, including suppression of VCAM1 expression and monocyte adhesion via AKT1/NOS3 signaling, further indicate a role in vascular homeostasis that could affect cardiac perfusion and remodeling.

Another protein that may connect inflammation with matrix signaling is SEMA7A. SEMA7A is notable because integrin signaling, inflammatory activation, and cell migration are all central to myocardial remodeling. In heart failure, inflammatory leukocyte recruitment and altered cell-matrix interactions contribute to fibrosis, microvascular dysfunction, and structural remodeling. Through promotion of focal adhesion complexes and pro-inflammatory cytokine production by monocytes and macrophages, SEMA7A could enhance the inflammatory-fibrotic axis that underlies progression of cardiac dysfunction. Its role in integrin-dependent signaling also makes it relevant to mechanotransduction, an important process in pressure-overload and dilated cardiomyopathy.

The next protein, SFRP1, introduces a signaling axis that has long been associated with cardiac remodeling. SFRP1 is important for heart failure biology because Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is a well-established regulator of cardiac development, fibroblast activation, hypertrophy, and post-injury remodeling. By antagonizing Wnt signals and lowering beta-catenin, SFRP1 may influence the balance between reparative healing and maladaptive fibrosis. Its antiproliferative effects on vascular cells and ability to modulate angiogenesis further strengthen its cardiovascular relevance. In the setting of heart failure, where both fibrotic remodeling and vascular rarefaction shape disease progression, SFRP1 may act as a key extracellular regulator of remodeling pathways.

In parallel with SFRP1, SMOC2 may also be relevant at the intersection of matrix organization and vascular adaptation. SMOC2 stands out because it combines extracellular matrix regulation with pro-angiogenic activity, both of which are highly relevant to heart failure progression. Cardiac remodeling depends on dynamic changes in matrix composition, while preservation or restoration of the microvasculature is critical for maintaining myocardial oxygen delivery. A protein that promotes matrix assembly and endothelial growth may influence scar organization, interstitial remodeling, and vascular adaptation after injury. Depending on context, such activity could support repair or contribute to maladaptive matrix accumulation, making SMOC2 a biologically plausible participant in heart failure pathogenesis.

Among extracellular matrix proteins, TNC appears especially relevant to active remodeling states. TNC is one of the most relevant extracellular matrix proteins in relation to heart failure because matrix remodeling and integrin-mediated signaling are central to ventricular adaptation and decompensation. Its ability to interact with multiple integrins suggests that it can modulate cell adhesion, mechanotransduction, and inflammatory remodeling in damaged tissue. The angiogenic functions of TNC also imply a role in vascular adaptation to stress. In the heart, extracellular matrix proteins that are re-expressed during injury often mark active remodeling and fibrosis, and TNC fits this pattern well as a candidate contributor to post-infarction remodeling and chronic heart failure progression.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

From matrix remodeling, the discussion returns to angiogenesis, where VEGFA is likely to have particularly direct relevance. VEGFA is arguably the most directly relevant protein on this list for heart failure because impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, and microvascular rarefaction are major determinants of myocardial ischemia, fibrosis, and contractile decline. VEGFA-driven endothelial survival and migration are essential for maintaining capillary density and supporting tissue repair after infarction or chronic pressure overload. Its activation of AKT, MAPK, FAK, and nitric oxide signaling also links it to cardioprotective vascular responses, perfusion regulation, and endothelial health. At the same time, excessive vascular permeability may contribute to congestion and edema, illustrating the complex, context-dependent role of VEGFA in heart failure pathophysiology.

Finally, although VWA1 is less directly connected to canonical heart failure mechanisms than several of the proteins above, it may still warrant consideration because of its structural role. Although less directly linked to canonical heart failure pathways than some other proteins listed, VWA1 remains potentially relevant because extracellular matrix assembly is fundamental to myocardial structural integrity. In heart failure, matrix disorganization contributes to chamber dilation, impaired force transmission, and abnormal tissue stiffness. Proteins involved in matrix assembly may therefore influence susceptibility to remodeling under chronic hemodynamic stress. Its role in muscle organization also raises the possibility that VWA1 participates more broadly in contractile tissue architecture, which could have indirect implications for cardiac function.
